New NadMesh Botnet Hunts Exposed AI Services for Cloud Keys and Kubernetes Tokens

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 13 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A Go botnet called NadMesh turned up in early July hunting exposed AI services, and the operator's own dashboard claims 3,811 unique AWS keys. A Shodan harvester keeps the scan queue stocked with ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Open WebUI, Langflow, and Gradio: the image generators, local model runners, and workflow builders that teams stand up fast and firewall late. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internet-exposed AI/Docker ports (8188/11434/7860/5678/2375) probed from public IPs · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposed AI service / Docker socket spawns shell + egress (NadMesh post-exploit)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] NadMesh hidden persistence file drops + cron in /dev/shm, /tmp, /etc/cron.d · [LLM] NadMesh agent sample execution by SHA1 31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New NadMesh Botnet Hunts Exposed AI Services for Cloud Keys and Kubernetes Token
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NadMesh C2 egress to 209.99.186.235 / cdnorigin.net · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud credential file harvest: reads of ~/.aws/config, .env, ~/.docker/config.json · [LLM] Kubernetes service-account token / kubeconfig theft on compromised host · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
NadMesh hidden persistence file drops + cron in /dev/shm, /tmp, /etc/cron.d AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact triple-persistence artefacts NadMesh writes on Linux hosts: hidden .a payloads under /dev/shm, /var/tmp and /tmp, hidden cron files /etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor and /etc/cron.d/.s, and rogue ~/.ssh/authorized_keys entries. These fixed paths are article-specific and rarely legitimate. Rationale: Uses the exact fixed drop paths XLab listed for NadMesh (/dev/shm/.a, /var/tmp/.a, /tmp/.a, /etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor, /etc/cron.d/.s, authorized_keys) — hidden filenames in these locations are near-zero-FP and survive the per-build hash randomisation the article warns about. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate configuration-management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) writing to /etc/cron.d — but named files there are not .sys_monitor or .s
  • Admin dropping a personal script to /tmp named .a (rare, hidden name)
  • Backup/AV tooling touching ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during key rotation
  • Container image build scripts writing to /dev/shm
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion") and FileName in (".sys_monitor",".s") == false)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the dropped file's contents and InitiatingProcess — a Go binary written by python/node/ollama or a shell spawned from an exposed service is confirmation. Cross-check the host for the C2 IOCs (209.99.186.235, cdnorigin.net). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host from the network before revoking anything. Kill all three persistence copies (payload, cron, authorized_keys) simultaneously — pulling one leaves the others to restore it. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate every AWS key, k8s SA token, .env and ~/.docker/config.json the host could read; revoke (not rotate) them, then review where they were used while live.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/tmp/") and FileName == ".a")
    or (FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d" and FileName in (".sys_monitor",".s"))
    or (FolderPath has "/.ssh/" and FileName == "authorized_keys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath in ("/dev/shm/.a","/var/tmp/.a","/tmp/.a","/etc/cron.d/.sys_monitor","/etc/cron.d/.s")
    or TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f2a1c4e-8d3b-4f7a-9c1e-2b5a7d9e0f11
description: Detects NadMesh dropping hidden .a payloads and hidden cron jobs used for triple persistence on Linux.
references:

detection:
  selection_hidden_payload:
    TargetFilename:

  selection_cron:

NadMesh C2 egress to 209.99.186.235 / cdnorigin.net AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host contacting NadMesh's confirmed command-and-control infrastructure — IP 209.99.186.235 or domain cdnorigin.net. Direct IOC match against XLab-published, second-source-confirmed C2. Rationale: Hard IOC match on the single C2 IP (209.99.186.235) and domain (cdnorigin.net) XLab published and gbhackers independently reported — deterministic, survives binary-hash rotation because the C2 endpoint is fixed. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate CDN sharing the cdnorigin.net name string in an unrelated hostname (validate exact domain)
  • Security researcher/sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel feed connector performing IOC validation lookups against the IP
  • Shared-hosting IP later re-purposed after takedown (check dates)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process — a shell/curl/Go binary reaching this IP from a server that runs ComfyUI/Ollama/Docker is a strong true positive. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and block 209.99.186.235 and cdnorigin.net at the egress firewall/DNS sinkhole. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the initiating process hash and parent to find the persistence drops (UC1), then revoke every cloud credential the host could access.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "209.99.186.235" or RemoteUrl has "cdnorigin.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "209.99.186.235" or Url has "cdnorigin.net"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, EventProduct),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "cdnorigin.net"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DnsQuery, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NadMesh agent sample execution by SHA1 31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or write of the one published NadMesh agent build by SHA1 hash. XLab notes each build is Garble+UPX+padding-randomised, so this catches only the disclosed sample — pair with the behavioural UCs for full coverage. Rationale: Deterministic SHA1 match on the single agent sample XLab released (confirmed by gbhackers). Low value alone because of per-build hash randomisation, but zero-FP and worth alerting; the article itself flags this limitation, which is why it's paired with behavioural UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst executing the sample in a lab connected to production EDR
  • Threat-intel retro-hunt tooling hashing quarantined files
  • No realistic benign execution of this exact hash
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host, user context and parent process of the execution. Step 2 (contain): Isolate immediately and preserve the binary for analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Because sibling builds have different hashes, pivot to behaviour — search the same host and peers for the persistence drops (UC1), C2 egress (UC2), and credential-file reads (UC4/UC5).
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA1 == "31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Kind="ProcessExec"),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA1 == "31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Kind="FileWrite")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA1 =~ "31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud credential file harvest: reads of ~/.aws/config, .env, ~/.docker/config.json AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NadMesh's core objective — a non-interactive/bot process reading AWS config/credentials, .env files, or the Docker registry config to steal cloud keys. Focuses on the exact files XLab says the bot ships home. Rationale: Targets the exact credential files XLab enumerates as NadMesh's loot (~/.aws/config, .env, ~/.docker/config.json) accessed via read/copy utilities — high-signal when the parent is an exposed AI service or a shell rather than an interactive admin session. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `cat ~/.aws/config` interactively during troubleshooting
  • CI/CD runner tar-ing a workspace that contains a .env file
  • Ansible/Terraform reading .aws/credentials for a legitimate deploy
  • Backup jobs archiving home directories including .docker/config.json
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","terraform","packer","aws") and AccountName !in~ ("nobody","www-data"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Check the parent process and user — a read spawned by ollama/python/node or an unattended shell (not an interactive TTY) is suspicious. Correlate with C2 egress on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate and revoke every AWS key, registry login and .env secret the host could read; the operator's dashboard already claimed 3,811 AWS keys, so assume compromise. Step 3 (hunt): Review CloudTrail for the exposed keys' usage while live, and check for k8s token access (UC5) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","head","tail","cp","tar","curl","strings","awk","sed","env","base64")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".aws/config",".aws/credentials",".docker/config.json") or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(^|[\s/])\.env($|[\s""])"
| where AccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ollama","python","python3","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cat","grep","head","tail","cp","tar","curl","strings","awk","sed","env","base64")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".aws/config",".aws/credentials",".docker/config.json") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(^|[\s/])\.env($|[\s""])"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kubernetes service-account token / kubeconfig theft on compromised host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts NadMesh reading the in-pod ServiceAccount token, its CA cert, or ~/.kube/config — the stated goal of acquiring 'Kubernetes cluster privileges'. Flags read/exfil utilities or curl-to-API touching these fixed paths. Rationale: Uses the canonical in-pod SA token path (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) and ~/.kube/config that XLab names as NadMesh loot; reads by curl/cat/base64 outside a legit kubectl workflow are high-fidelity token theft signals. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate in-cluster app reading its own SA token to call the API (very common — scope to non-app utilities)
  • kubectl config operations by an on-call engineer
  • Helm/operators mounting and reading the token path
  • Monitoring agents (Prometheus/Datadog) reading the SA token
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("kubelet","prometheus","node_exporter","datadog-agent") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the reader is the workload's own service or an ad-hoc shell/curl; a base64/curl piping the token to an external IP is confirmation. Step 2 (contain): Delete/rotate the affected ServiceAccount token, cordon the node, and revoke any derived cluster credentials. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the K8s audit log (UC7) for secret enumeration or ClusterRoleBinding creation from that SA, and check other pods on the node for the same reads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token","/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt",".kube/config")
| where FileName in~ ("cat","curl","wget","grep","head","cp","tar","base64","env","kubectl","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token","/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt",".kube/config")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cat","curl","wget","grep","head","cp","tar","base64","env","kubectl","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kubernetes ServiceAccount Token or Kubeconfig Read
id: d4b7e290-3f16-4c8a-9e51-0a2b6c8d1f34
description: Detects command-line reads of the in-pod Kubernetes ServiceAccount token or kubeconfig, matching NadMesh cluster-credential theft.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html
  - https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/18
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1528
  - attack.t1552.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/cat'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/grep'
      - '/head'
      - '/base64'
      - '/tar'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token'
      - '.kube/config'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_path
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token* OR */var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt* OR *.kube/config*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(cat|curl|wget|grep|head|cp|tar|base64|env|kubectl|sh|bash)$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/var\/run\/secrets\/kubernetes\.io\/serviceaccount\/(token|ca\.crt)|\.kube\/config)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token*" OR Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt*" OR Processes.process="*.kube/config*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token*" OR Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt*" OR Processes.process="*.kube/config*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Exposed AI service / Docker socket spawns shell + egress (NadMesh post-exploit) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE step: an exposed AI/MCP service (ComfyUI/Gradio/Langflow/Open WebUI/Ollama/n8n) or the Docker API on 2375 spawning /bin/sh, curl or wget that reaches out — the execute_command / docker_containers_api_rce chain XLab observed. High-value parent→child pivot. Rationale: Encodes the specific victim software XLab names (ComfyUI/Ollama/Langflow/Open WebUI/n8n/Gradio and Docker on 2375) as the parent, paired with shell/download children and the article's C2/drop-path strings — the parent+child combination is what turns a normal service into a detection. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An n8n/Node workflow legitimately shelling out to curl an API
  • ComfyUI custom-node installer invoking pip/curl during setup
  • Docker entrypoint scripts running chmod/curl on container start
  • Ollama model pull that fetches over HTTP
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","pip3 install","ollama pull","npm install") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("209.99.186.235","cdnorigin.net","/dev/shm/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the child command line — a fetch of a payload to /dev/shm or a connection to 209.99.186.235 is confirmation; a benign pip/model pull is not. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, and get the exposed service behind auth or off the public internet (ports 8188/11434/7860/5678/2375). Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host for persistence drops (UC1), credential reads (UC4/UC5) and C2 (UC2); auto-blacklisting means the operator moves fast once a host responds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ollama","python","python3","node","dockerd","docker-proxy","containerd-shim")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("comfyui","langflow","open-webui","openwebui","n8n","gradio")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/tmp/.","209.99.186.235","cdnorigin.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ollama","python","node","dockerd","docker-proxy","containerd-shim")
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("comfyui","langflow","open-webui","openwebui","n8n","gradio")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","perl")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","/dev/shm/","/var/tmp/","/tmp/.","209.99.186.235","cdnorigin.net")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Exposed AI Service or Docker Socket Spawns Shell with Egress
id: 5e0c2a48-9f71-4b36-a2d9-3c7e1b8f4a62
description: Detects ComfyUI/Ollama/n8n/Langflow/Docker daemon spawning a shell or download utility that fetches or executes a remote payload, matching NadMesh RCE.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html
  - https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/ollama'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
      - '/dockerd'
      - '/docker-proxy'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
  selection_action:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'curl'
      - 'wget'
      - 'chmod'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - '209.99.186.235'
      - 'cdnorigin.net'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_action
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */dash OR */curl OR */wget) @process.command_line:(*curl* OR *wget* OR *chmod* OR */dev/shm/* OR *209.99.186.235* OR *cdnorigin.net*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(ollama|python3?|node|dockerd|docker-proxy|containerd-shim)/i ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|chmod|perl)$/i
| CommandLine=/(curl|wget|chmod|\/dev\/shm\/|\/var\/tmp\/|209\.99\.186\.235|cdnorigin\.net)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("ollama","python","python3","node","dockerd","docker-proxy","containerd-shim") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","perl") AND (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*chmod*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/shm/*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*209.99.186.235*" OR Processes.process="*cdnorigin.net*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("ollama","python","python3","node","dockerd","docker-proxy","containerd-shim") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","perl") AND (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*chmod*" OR Processes.process="*/dev/shm/*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/*" OR Processes.process="*209.99.186.235*" OR Processes.process="*cdnorigin.net*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Internet-exposed AI/Docker ports (8188/11434/7860/5678/2375) probed from public IPs AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces the reconnaissance surface NadMesh's rescan job hits first: inbound public connections to ComfyUI (8188), Ollama (11434), Gradio (7860), n8n (5678) and the Docker API (2375). Flags hosts fielding scans on multiple such ports or from many source IPs. Rationale: Uses the four rescan-priority ports the article explicitly lists (8188 ComfyUI, 11434 Ollama, 7860 Gradio, 5678 n8n) plus Docker 2375; an internet-facing host taking multi-port or multi-source hits on these is exactly the exposure NadMesh's Shodan harvester feeds on. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-nadmesh-botnet-hunts-exposed-ai.html • https://gbhackers.com/new-nadmesh-botnet/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users accessing an intentionally-published Ollama/ComfyUI demo from many office IPs
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) sweeping these ports
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting the service port
  • CDN/uptime-monitoring services probing the endpoint
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("ml-demo-public","ollama-sandbox")   // allowlist intentionally-public demo hosts
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host truly should be internet-facing on these ports and whether the sources are known scanners vs. your users. Step 2 (contain): Put the service behind authentication or a VPN/allowlist — the article stresses no patch closes exposed-service abuse. Step 3 (hunt): For any host that also shows a post-exploit shell (UC6) or credential reads (UC4/UC5), treat as compromised and escalate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where LocalPort in (8188, 11434, 7860, 5678, 2375)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Conns=count(), SrcIPs=dcount(RemoteIP), Ports=make_set(LocalPort) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where SrcIPs > 5 or array_length(Ports) >= 2   // >5 distinct external scanners/hr or >=2 exposed AI ports hit
| order by Conns desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| where DstPortNumber in (8188, 11434, 7860, 5678, 2375)
| summarize Conns=count(), SrcIPs=dcount(SrcIpAddr), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where SrcIPs > 5 or array_length(Ports) >= 2   // >5 distinct external scanners/hr or >=2 exposed AI ports hit
| order by Conns desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1 (LocalPort=8188 OR LocalPort=11434 OR LocalPort=7860 OR LocalPort=5678 OR LocalPort=2375)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, LocalPort], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true), limit=max)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(All_Traffic.src) as SrcIPs values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as Ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8188,11434,7860,5678,2375) by All_Traffic.dest _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)` | where SrcIPs > 5 OR mvcount(Ports) >= 2
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(All_Traffic.src) as SrcIPs values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as Ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" All_Traffic.dest_port IN (8188,11434,7860,5678,2375) by All_Traffic.dest _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)` | where SrcIPs > 5 OR mvcount(Ports) >= 2
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-41176", "CVE-2022-22947", "CVE-2017-12611")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-41176", "CVE-2022-22947", "CVE-2017-12611")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or SHA1 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or MD5 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or SHA1 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec") or MD5 in~ ("31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["31c69b3e12936abca770d430066f379ec1d997ec"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoldenEyeDog Subgroup Linked to DigiCert Breach and Code-Signing Certificate Theft

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have attributed the April 2026 DigiCert security incident to a threat activity cluster dubbed CylindricalCanine. Expel, which shared technical details of the event, described the threat actor as a sub-group of GoldenEyeDog (aka APT-Q-27, Dragon Breath, and Miuuti Group), a Chinese cybercrime group known for its targeting of the gambling and gaming sectors using

Golden Gh0st Loader DLL side-load loading encrypted 'update.log' payload from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the CylindricalCanine/GoldenEyeDog DLL side-loading chain where a legitimate signed EXE dropped into a user-writable directory loads a co-located rogue DLL that then reads an encrypted payload named update.log. Correlates the anomalous image-load from AppData/Temp/Public with the update.log payload drop on the same host within 30 minutes. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific side-load pattern (legit EXE + co-located rogue DLL in user-writable path) plus the distinctive encrypted payload filename update.log; the same-host temporal join to the DLL image-load makes it high-fidelity. update.log filename is from the primary Expel/THN reporting; side-loading chain corroborated by Elastic RONINGLOADER analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/roningloader
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/self-contained legitimate apps (e.g. Zoom, some updaters) that ship DLLs beside the EXE in AppData
  • Software installers extracting to %TEMP% that transiently load their own DLLs
  • Log-rotation tools that legitimately create files literally named update.log near an app in ProgramData
  • Developer build output directories under user profiles containing DLLs and .log files
  • EDR/AV self-updaters staging DLLs in ProgramData
Suppression filter
| where SideloadExe !in~ ("zoom.exe","teams.exe","update.exe","setup.exe") and SideloadExeFolder !has "\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the SideloadExe hash/signature and RogueDll hash; verify whether the EXE is a known legit vendor binary running from an abnormal path and whether the DLL is unsigned. Inspect PayloadPath (update.log) size/entropy — encrypted blob is high-entropy. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host, kill the sideload process tree, and quarantine the EXE+DLL+update.log triad. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep the org for the same RogueDll hash and for outbound WebSocket traffic to qaqkongtiao.com or the GoldenEyeDog IP set from the same devices.
let Window = 14d; let SideloadHosts = DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(Window) | where FileName endswith ".dll" | where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\") | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\") | project DllLoadTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, SideloadExe=InitiatingProcessFileName, SideloadExeFolder=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RogueDll=FileName, DllFolder=FolderPath; DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(Window) | where FileName =~ "update.log" | where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\") | project PayloadTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, PayloadPath=FolderPath, PayloadWriter=InitiatingProcessFileName | join kind=inner SideloadHosts on DeviceId | where abs(datetime_diff('minute', DllLoadTime, PayloadTime)) <= 30 | project PayloadTime, DllLoadTime, DeviceName, SideloadExe, SideloadExeFolder, RogueDll, DllFolder, PayloadPath, PayloadWriter | order by PayloadTime desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where TargetFileName =~ "update.log" | where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\Users\\Public\\", "\\ProgramData\\", "\\Temp\\") | where ActingProcessName !has "\\Windows\\" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath | order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\update.log OR *\\Update.log OR *\\UPDATE.LOG) @TargetFilename:(*\\AppData\\* OR *\\appdata\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Public\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)

GoldenEyeDog .scr screensaver payload executed from download/archive path (support-chat delivery) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the DigiCert-style delivery where a ZIP disguised as a customer screenshot contains a .scr executable delivered via a support/chat channel. Flags execution of any .scr binary from Downloads/Temp/AppData/Desktop or spawned by an archive tool, browser, or Outlook, excluding legitimate System32 screensavers. Rationale: Directly models the article's stated delivery: a ZIP 'disguised as a customer screenshot' containing a .scr executable sent through a support chat channel. .scr execution outside System32 is inherently rare, and the download/archive-parent constraint plus Windows-dir exclusion keeps FPs manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/digicert-hacked-screensaver/ • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy corporate screensavers copied to Desktop/AppData by users
  • GPO-deployed .scr screensavers staged in a profile path before relocation
  • Users double-clicking a .scr sample for testing from Downloads
  • Third-party screensaver apps installed under AppData
  • Security-team detonation of .scr samples on analyst workstations
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","grpconv.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Retrieve the .scr SHA256 and check reputation; confirm the parent (archive tool / Outlook / browser) and the originating file (ZIP named like a screenshot). Review the user's recent support-chat / email context. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host, kill the .scr process tree, quarantine the .scr and its source archive. Step 3 (Hunt): Search mail/chat gateways for ZIP attachments named as screenshots to support staff, and pivot the host for follow-on DLL side-load (update.log) and C2 to qaqkongtiao.com.

Golden Gh0st RAT plaintext WebSocket C2 to qaqkongtiao.com / GoldenEyeDog IP set AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host beaconing to the hardcoded CylindricalCanine C2 domain qaqkongtiao.com or the campaign's known C2 IP addresses. Golden Gh0st RAT uses unencrypted WebSocket traffic, so these connections are directly attributable command-and-control. Rationale: qaqkongtiao.com is confirmed by a second source as the hardcoded C2 domain; any resolution/connection is high-fidelity. The seven IPs are the campaign C2 set — connections to them from endpoints are directly actionable. Plaintext WebSocket C2 (per Expel) means no TLS SNI evasion. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/ • https://otx.alienvault.com/browse/global/pulses?q=tag%3A%22GoldenEyeDog%22
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sinkhole/DNS-RPZ redirection making qaqkongtiao.com resolve to a benign sinkhole IP
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox VM in the environment deliberately connecting to the C2 for research
  • IP reassignment — a C2 IP later rehosting a benign service (validate first-seen against reporting date)
  • Security scanner probing the IP set from a SOC jump box
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName) making the connection and whether it is a signed legit binary (likely side-load host) or the update.log-loaded stage. Confirm plaintext WebSocket over the connection port. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host, block qaqkongtiao.com and the IP set at proxy/firewall, kill the C2 process. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on all hosts that resolved the domain, then sweep those hosts for the DLL side-load (update.log) and .scr delivery artifacts.

Golden Gh0st RAT browser/credential collection targeting 360, QQ and Skype data stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts non-browser processes accessing the credential/profile stores of the specific applications Golden Gh0st RAT harvests — 360 Secure/Speed Browser, Tencent QQ Browser, and Skype. Presence of the Chinese browser directories being read by an unexpected process is a strong stealer signal in APAC finance environments. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit list of Golden Gh0st RAT collection targets; the Chinese-market browsers (360 Secure/Speed, Tencent QQ Browser) are rare in corporate APAC finance estates, so a non-browser process reading their profiles is a distinctive stealer indicator that separates this from generic Chrome/Firefox credential-theft rules. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync agents (OneDrive, corporate DLP) enumerating profile folders
  • Endpoint migration/USMT tooling copying user browser data
  • Antivirus full-disk scans opening browser store files
  • IT scripts inventorying installed browsers
  • Legit third-party password managers importing from 360/QQ browsers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","usmtutils.exe","scanutil.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the InitiatingProcess and its hash/path; determine if it is a signed backup/DLP agent or an unknown binary from a user-writable path. Check for concurrent archive creation (staging) on the host. Step 2 (Contain): If the process is unknown/unsigned, isolate the host, kill and quarantine it, and force-rotate credentials for accounts on that device. Step 3 (Hunt): Correlate the same InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet and check those hosts for update.log side-load and C2 to qaqkongtiao.com.

Execution of stolen-cert-signed Zhong Stealer / Golden Gh0st RAT artifacts by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any process execution, file write, or DLL load matching the known SHA256 hashes of Zhong Stealer / Golden Gh0st malware weaponized with the fraudulently obtained DigiCert EV code-signing certificates. Because these binaries carry a valid Authenticode signature, hash matching (not signer trust) is the reliable detection. Rationale: Defender AH exposes no Authenticode signer column, so the reviewer's DigiCert-signer / issuer-transition hypotheses aren't directly expressible; hash matching against the campaign's known Zhong Stealer / Golden Gh0st artifacts is the reliable equivalent and self-validating (SHA256 collisions are infeasible). Hashes are from the article's IOC set; confidence is Medium pending independent hash corroboration. Cross-checked against: • https://expel.com/blog/introducing-cylindricalcanine/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goldeneyedog-subgroup-linked-to.html
ATT&CKT1553.002 T1588.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Effectively none — a full SHA256 match cannot be a benign collision
  • A retro-hunt matching a quarantined/already-remediated copy of the sample (validate the event is live execution, not AV quarantine handling)
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in the same tenant
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Confirm the event is live execution/write (not AV quarantine) and capture the host, user, and full path. Note the Authenticode signer — expect a revoked DigiCert EV cert. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the host immediately, kill/quarantine the artifact, and treat any credentials used on the host as compromised. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep the org for these hashes across process/file/image-load telemetry, pivot to the C2 IOCs (qaqkongtiao.com and IP set), and check for the update.log side-load and .scr delivery on the same devices.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")

let BadHashes = dynamic(["da2c58308e860e57df4c46465fd1cfc68d41e8699b4871e9a9be3c434283d50b", "82794015e2b40cc6e02d3c1d50241465c0cf2c2e4f0a7a2a8f880edaee203724", "c65170be2bf4f0bd71b9044592c063eaa82f3d43fcbd8a81e30a959bcaad8ae5", "2515b546125d20013237aeadec5873e6438ada611347035358059a77a32c54f5", "1613a913d0384cbb958e9a8d6b00fffaf77c27d348ebc7886d6c563a6f22f2b7", "395f835731d25803a791db984062dd5cfdcade6f95cc5d0f68d359af32f6258d", "1c1528b546aa29be6614707cbe408cb4b46e8ed05bf3fe6b388b9f22a4ee37e2", "4d5beb8efd4ade583c8ff730609f142550e8ed14c251bae1097c35a756ed39e6", "96f401b80d3319f8285fa2bb7f0d66ca9055d349c044b78c27e339bcfb07cdf0", "33b494eaaa6d7ed75eec74f8c8c866b6c42f59ca72b8517b3d4752c3313e617c", "fc63f5dfc93f2358f4cba18cbdf99578fff5dac4cdd2de193a21f6041a0e01bc", "fd4dd9904549c6655465331921a28330ad2b9ff1c99eb993edf2252001f1d107", "3dd470e85fe77cd847ca59d1d08ec8ccebe9bd73fd2cf074c29d87ca2fd24e33"]);

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Coding Tests Deliver OtterCookie-Aligned Malware Hidden in SVG Flag Images

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 8 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

North Korean threat actors linked to the Contagious Interview campaign have been observed employing steganography in SVG image files to conceal malicious payloads as part of a campaign using fake job postings and coding challenges. Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Fake Coding Tests Deliver OtterCookie-Aligned Malware Hidden in SVG Flag Images
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts a node.exe/npm process resolving or connecting to the REF9403 command-and-control infrastructure (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) used by the OtterCookie-aligned four-stage payload. Node is not a browser, so an interpreter reaching this dev-TLD domain family is a high-fidelity C2 signal specific to the fake-coding-test lure. Rationale: Anchors on the four confirmed C2 subdomains (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) plus a node/npm initiator so it fires on interpreter-driven C2 even though the domain is single-sourced to Elastic; a JS runtime resolving a dev-TLD attacker domain is near-zero in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/11/contagious-interview-malware-delivered-through-fake-developer-job-interviews/ • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using a package or SaaS hosted on a *.rightwidth.dev subdomain (validate the specific FQDN against the IOC list)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned analysis VM
  • Corporate proxy/DNS-sinkhole re-resolving the domain for blocking (resolver IP, not endpoint)
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling actively resolving IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "rightwidth.dev" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("threatintel","ioc-check","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node/npm and pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to find the trojanized repo path; check whether the host cloned a repo referencing Next.js v14/NestJS/Auth.js lure stack. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block *.rightwidth.dev at DNS/proxy, and kill the node process tree; preserve the repo and node_modules for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for reads of .claude/.cursor/.windsurf dirs, browser Login Data, and crypto-wallet extension storage, and rotate any credentials/AI-service tokens present on the host.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "rightwidth.dev" or RemoteUrl in~ ("ldb.rightwidth.dev","upload.rightwidth.dev","controller.rightwidth.dev","rightwidth.dev")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DnsQuery endswith "rightwidth.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Node.js process enumerating the AI coding-tool configuration directories (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .windsurf, .pearai, .llama) that OtterCookie's file-stealer module explicitly harvests for API keys, tokens and LLM conversation logs. This directory set touched by a JS interpreter is the novel differentiator in the REF9403 campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact six AI-tool config dir names OtterCookie enumerates (corroborated by Talos and cyberandramen.net) with a node.exe initiator; a JS runtime crawling .claude/.cursor/.windsurf together is behaviour no legitimate build tool exhibits. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The AI tools themselves updating their config (initiating process is cursor.exe/claude.exe, not node.exe)
  • A developer's own dotfile-sync or backup script running under node reading these dirs
  • VS Code extensions built on Node performing legitimate config reads of a single tool
  • Security tooling inventorying installed AI extensions
Suppression filter
| where DirsTouched >= 2 and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dotfiles-sync"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate access reads one tool dir; OtterCookie sweeps all six plus .env/.pem/.key/.ssh. Confirm the parent is an npm-launched project, not the AI IDE. 2) Contain: isolate host, suspend the node process, and immediately rotate all AI-service API tokens (Claude/Cursor/Gemini) and any secrets found in the swept directories. 3) Hunt: correlate with rightwidth.dev C2 (UC1) and serverValidation.js execution (UC3) on the same host, and check for browser Login Data / crypto-wallet extension reads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount=dcount(FileName), DirsTouched=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| summarize FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath), Dirs=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the OtterCookie loader serverValidation.js, which reassembles the base64 payload fragments hidden in HTML comments across the country-flag SVG images (AE.svg, AF.svg) in the repo's assets directory. Detection targets the named loader script running under node as part of the fake coding-assessment repo. Rationale: Uses the exact loader filename serverValidation.js named by Elastic plus a node interpreter; dual proc+filewrite Defender coverage catches both cmdline-visible and require()-loaded execution, so the detection survives whether the script is passed as an arg or imported. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korea-linked-hackers-hide.html • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely shipping an unrelated file named serverValidation.js (verify repo origin and whether it reads SVG assets)
  • Developer authoring server-side validation logic in a file coincidentally named the same
  • CI/CD pipeline running a benign validation step under node
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the parent repo dir, inspect the assets/ folder for country-flag SVGs (AE.svg, AF.svg) containing base64 in HTML comments, and read serverValidation.js for base64 reassembly/eval logic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node tree, quarantine the repo, and block rightwidth.dev. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same repo/loader across other developer endpoints (Slack-lure victims), and pivot to UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 AI-config-dir reads; rotate credentials on any confirmed host.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="proc", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="filewrite", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-17 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A technical analysis of three chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Siemens ROX II OT switches that allow privilege escalation and persistent root access. The post Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy appeared first on Unit 42 .

CVEsCVE-2025-40947 CVE-2025-40948 CVE-2025-40949
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.001 T1190

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) · [LLM] Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2025-40948 stage where a root-privileged xz utility is misused with decompress-to-stdout flags to read sensitive files (/etc/shadow, SSH/TLS private keys, config) on a Ruggedcom ROX II OT switch. Article-specific: xz functioning like cat against credential-bearing files is the reconnaissance foothold of the chain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE-2025-40948 mechanic — root-privileged xz used like cat (decompress-to-stdout) against password hashes and private keys. Pairing xz with a sensitive-file target and a stdout/decompress flag makes it high-fidelity; xz legitimately never streams /etc/shadow. Cross-checked NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1003.008 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decompressing a .xz log/backup archive with xz -dc to a pager
  • Firmware/update tooling that pipes xz -d output during a package install
  • A monitoring script that reads a config file that happens to end in .key but is not a private key
  • Backup jobs streaming compressed archives from /etc via xz
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("backup","firmware","/var/log/") and not SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full Syslog/auditd EXECVE line — confirm the xz target is /etc/shadow, an SSH/TLS private key, or a credential config, and identify the invoking user/session on the ROX II switch. 2) Contain: isolate the switch's management plane (block untrusted access to the web/CLI mgmt VLAN), rotate any exposed device keys/passwords, and confirm firmware is upgraded to V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: on the same device look for the follow-on chain — feature-key command injection (CVE-2025-40947) and root crontab modification (CVE-2025-40949) within the following minutes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "xz" or SyslogMessage has "xz"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key")
