Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40947: an attacker-controlled feature-key payload submitted to the ROX II web/CLI management is inserted unsanitized into a root-privileged command, allowing shell command injection. Article-specific: feature-key validation input carrying shell metacharacters is the privilege-escalation pivot of the chain. Rationale: Grounded in the CVE-2025-40947 description — an unsanitized feature-key payload inserted directly into a root command. Detecting shell metacharacters (;, |, &&, $(), backtick, $IFS) inside a feature-key request/log line is high-fidelity because a legitimate feature key is an opaque signed token with no shell syntax. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin pasting a legitimate feature key that coincidentally contains a semicolon-delimited field
  • WAF/proxy URL-decoding artifacts that surface encoded characters in benign query strings
  • Automated inventory tooling querying the feature-key endpoint without injection payloads
  • Penetration-test / vulnerability-scanner traffic fuzzing the mgmt interface
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys") or ProcessName has_any ("nessus","scan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: reconstruct the feature-key request/log entry — confirm shell metacharacters are inside the attacker-controlled key field rather than a benign token, and identify the authenticated user and source IP. 2) Contain: revoke the session, restrict the ROX II management interface to a trusted jump host, and verify firmware V2.17.1 is applied (the fix). 3) Hunt: check for a preceding CVE-2025-40948 xz file read and a following CVE-2025-40949 root crontab write on the same device to confirm full-chain execution; capture any commands spawned as root.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key"
| where SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "| " or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "feature-key" (";sh" OR "&&" OR "|sh" OR "|bash" OR "$IFS" OR "; /")
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*feature*key*" OR Web.uri_path="*featurekey*" OR Web.uri_path="*feature-key*") (Web.uri_query="*;*" OR Web.uri_query="*$(*" OR Web.uri_query="*|*" OR Web.uri_query="*&&*" OR Web.uri_query="*%3B*" OR Web.uri_query="*%24%28*" OR Web.uri_query="*%60*" OR Web.url="*%3B*" OR Web.url="*%24%28*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.uri_query Web.http_user_agent Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40949: an authenticated attacker abuses the ROX II web management task scheduler to inject commands into the root crontab, establishing reboot-surviving persistence. Article-specific: new root cron entries executing network-fetch or /tmp payloads are the persistence stage of the chain. Rationale: Maps to the CVE-2025-40949 mechanic — injected commands in the root cron table via the web scheduler. Cron parentage plus a remote-fetch/shell payload is high-fidelity: legitimate ROX II cron jobs do not curl/wget from /tmp or spawn reverse shells. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled maintenance job that uses curl/wget to pull an update from an internal server
  • Vendor diagnostic cron task writing to /tmp
  • Admin-created backup cron entry piping data out via a shell
  • Config-management agent (e.g. an internal orchestration script) launched from cron
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("/opt/siemens/","internal-update") and RemoteHostAllowlisted == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the current root crontab and the ROX II task-scheduler audit entry — confirm the offending job was created via the web scheduler and points at an external host or /tmp payload. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron entry, kill any spawned payload process, isolate the switch's mgmt plane, and upgrade to firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: correlate backward to the CVE-2025-40947 feature-key injection and CVE-2025-40948 xz disclosure on the same device, and sweep other ROX II switches for identical cron entries or callback destinations.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility =~ "cron" or ProcessName has_any ("crontab","crond","CRON")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget","curl","/tmp/","bash -i","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d","nc ") or SyslogMessage contains "$("
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SyslogMessage, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) AIExploitation High
Correlates the three chained ROX II exploit stages — xz file disclosure, feature-key command injection, and root cron persistence — observed on the same switch within a short window. Article-specific: alerts on the documented 'three steps to the terminal' progression rather than any single stage in isolation. Rationale: Encodes the article's core thesis — the 'three steps to the terminal' chain — by requiring ≥2 distinct documented stages (xz disclosure, feature-key injection, root cron persistence) on one ROX II switch within a 10-minute bin, which is far higher-fidelity than any single-stage alert. Datadog query surfaces the indicators; the count/window is applied at rule level. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test replaying the full chain against a lab ROX II
  • Vendor validation run of the V2.17.1 patch that exercises xz, feature-key and scheduler code paths
  • Noisy vulnerability scanner touching all three mgmt endpoints in one sweep
  • A single benign admin session that legitimately reads a config, sets a feature key, and edits a cron job in quick succession
Suppression filter
| where not (Computer has_any ("lab","test","staging") or HostIP in ("127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the correlated evidence set and confirm the stages are attacker-driven (sensitive-file xz read, metacharacters in feature-key, remote/tmp cron payload) rather than benign admin work; identify the switch, user and source IP. 2) Contain: isolate the switch management plane, revoke the session, remove any malicious cron entry, rotate exposed device credentials/keys, and enforce firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP and callback destinations across all ROX II / Ruggedcom devices for identical chain activity and stage-3 persistence artifacts.
let Window = 10m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend Stage = case(
    SyslogMessage has "xz" and SyslogMessage has_any("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key"), "1-disclosure",
    (SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key") and (SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"), "2-cmdinjection",
    (ProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","crontab") or Facility =~ "cron") and (SyslogMessage has_any("wget","curl","/tmp/","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d") or SyslogMessage contains "$("), "3-persistence",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Stage)
| summarize Stages = make_set(Stage), StageCount = dcount(Stage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Evidence = make_list(SyslogMessage, 20) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where StageCount >= 2   // >=2 of the 3 documented stages on one switch inside a 10m bin
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog ("xz" OR "feature-key" OR "crontab") ("id_rsa" OR "shadow" OR ";sh" OR "&&" OR "wget" OR "curl" OR "/tmp/")
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*xz*" OR Processes.process="*feature*key*" OR Processes.parent_process_name=cron OR Processes.parent_process_name=crond) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval stage=case(match(process,"(?i)xz.*(shadow|id_rsa|id_dsa|private|\.key|\.pem)"),"1-disclosure", match(process,"(?i)feature.?key") AND match(process,"[;|&`$]"),"2-cmdinjection", (parent_process_name="cron" OR parent_process_name="crond") AND match(process,"(?i)(wget|curl|/tmp/|bash -i|/dev/tcp/|base64 -d)"),"3-persistence", true(),null()) | where isnotnull(stage) | stats dc(stage) as stage_count values(stage) as stages values(process) as processes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where stage_count>=2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*xz*" OR Processes.process="*feature*key*" OR Processes.parent_process_name=cron OR Processes.parent_process_name=crond) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval stage=case(match(process,"(?i)xz.*(shadow|id_rsa|id_dsa|private|\.key|\.pem)"),"1-disclosure", match(process,"(?i)feature.?key") AND match(process,"[;|&`$]"),"2-cmdinjection", (parent_process_name="cron" OR parent_process_name="crond") AND match(process,"(?i)(wget|curl|/tmp/|bash -i|/dev/tcp/|base64 -d)"),"3-persistence", true(),null()) | where isnotnull(stage) | stats dc(stage) as stage_count values(stage) as stages values(process) as processes min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where stage_count>=2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-16 18 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

From late April 2026 to mid-June 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed increased ACR Stealer activity across customer environments. These campaigns are successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise environments. The post ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix RunMRU entry launching rundll32 against WebDAV GUID share (ACR Stealer) · [LLM] MSHTA remote HTA launched by explorer→powershell chain (ACR Stealer fileless campaign) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint traffic to ACR Stealer C2 / dead-drop domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

ClickFix RunMRU entry launching rundll32 against WebDAV GUID share (ACR Stealer) AIDelivery High
Hunts the ACR Stealer ClickFix initial-access artifact: a Run-dialog (RunMRU) history value in which the pasted command drives cmd.exe/rundll32.exe to load a DLL from a remote WebDAV share addressed as a `@ssl` UNC path with a GUID directory. This is the on-disk fingerprint left when a victim pastes the ClickFix command, before any child process runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Block 1 RunMRU logic plus the corroborated `@ssl\<GUID>\` WebDAV UNC form; RunMRU only records manually pasted Run-dialog commands, so rundll32+@ssl+GUID there is near-zero-FP evidence of ClickFix paste-execution. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1218.011 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legitimate admin scripting that maps a WebDAV DAVWWWRoot share via rundll32 (uncommon in enterprise)
  • Security researcher / red team replaying the ClickFix chain in a sandbox
  • Backup or MDM tooling that writes synthetic RunMRU entries (very rare)
  • Manual analyst reproduction of the IOC on a triage box
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RegistryValueData and extract the WebDAV host + GUID; confirm it matches sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net or another external host, and check whether a rundll32.exe process with that UNC path actually spawned. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, block the WebDAV host/domain at proxy and DNS, and kill any rundll32/pythonw child processes. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the follow-on %LocalAppData%\Temp deceptive dir, the 'Autoupdate' scheduled task, and outbound traffic to the ACR C2 domains.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_all ("rundll32", "@ssl")
| where RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)@ssl\\[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}\\"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("start", "pushd", ",#1", ".google")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_all ("rundll32", "@ssl")
| where RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)@ssl\\[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

rundll32 loading DLL from remote WebDAV @ssl GUID share with ordinal export (ACR Stealer) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 execution step where rundll32.exe loads a DLL directly from a remote WebDAV share (UNC `\\host@SSL\<GUID>\<name>.google,#1`) over HTTPS. Matches the exact confirmed sample cmdline against sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net and the GUID directory + `,#1` ordinal export. Rationale: Uses the externally-confirmed exact cmdline shape (`rundll32.exe \\sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net\<GUID>\...google,#1`): rundll32 loading a DLL over a WebDAV @ssl UNC with a GUID dir and `,#N` ordinal export is not seen in benign activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise apps that legitimately load resources from a mapped WebDAV/DAVWWWRoot path via rundll32 (rare)
  • Penetration test or purple-team replay of the ACR chain
  • Software installer that side-loads a DLL from an internal SharePoint WebDAV mount (would lack the external GUID host)
  • EDR sensor telemetry replays during IR reproduction
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the WebDAV host is external and non-corporate, capture the GUID path and DLL name, and check for a preceding cmd.exe/pushd parent and RunMRU paste. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the WebDAV domain/IP at proxy+DNS, and terminate rundll32 and any spawned pythonw.exe. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same GUID host or `,#1` ordinal pattern, and for the LogiOptionsPlus temp dir and 'Autoupdate' scheduled task on affected hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i),#\d+\s*$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@ssl" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","looksta.icu")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i),#\d+\s*$"
| where (CommandLine has "@ssl" or CommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net","creativecommunityinfo.art","enhanceblabber.cc","looksta.icu"))
| where CommandLine matches regex @"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MSHTA remote HTA launched by explorer→powershell chain (ACR Stealer fileless campaign) AIDelivery High
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-2 fileless chain: explorer.exe spawns a bare powershell.exe which invokes mshta.exe against a remote HTTPS URL whose path is a 7-digit numeric token. Matches the article's exact process-tree and cmdline shape for the MSHTA/steganography route. Rationale: Directly implements the article's Block 3 process-tree (explorer→powershell→mshta) plus the remote HTTPS HTA with a 7-digit path token; mshta fetching a remote URL from a PowerShell parent is a strong LOLBin proxy-execution signal specific to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/acr-stealer-uses-clickfix-lures-to.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.001 T1204.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB app delivered as a remote HTA via a launcher script (rare, and usually internal host not HTTPS/7-digit path)
  • Red-team ClickFix simulation
  • Admin troubleshooting that manually runs mshta against a URL
  • IT automation using mshta for a hosted config page
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the mshta URL, detonate/inspect it for the steganographic PNG stage, and confirm the explorer→powershell parentage indicates a paste-run rather than scripted automation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the HTA URL/domain, and kill mshta plus any in-memory child. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on obfuscated PowerShell, VirtualAlloc/Fiber-API in-memory execution, and browser credential-store access on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "explorer.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine in~ ('"PowerShell.exe" ', '"PowerShell.exe"')
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "https://" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex "/[0-9]{7}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has "https://" and CommandLine matches regex "/[0-9]{7}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Masqueraded 'Autoupdate' scheduled task run by PowerShell loader (ACR Stealer persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 persistence/updater behavior where the obfuscated PowerShell loader invokes schtasks to run a hidden task named 'Autoupdate' suffixed with an 8-digit numeric token, disguised as a legitimate software update triggering at user sign-in. Rationale: Implements the article's Block 2 exactly: a PowerShell parent driving schtasks against a task named 'Autoupdate' with an 8-digit token is a specific masqueraded-update persistence artifact, far narrower than generic scheduled-task creation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-warns-of-surge-in-acr-stealer-attacks-on-customers/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.001 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software updaters that create tasks literally named 'Autoupdate' via a PowerShell installer (check the parent chain and signer)
  • Endpoint management/RMM tooling scripting scheduled tasks named with build numbers
  • Internal packaging scripts that name update tasks with date-stamps (8 digits)
  • Admin manually registering an update task through a PS console
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AppData\\Local\\Temp", "pythonw", "LogiOptionsPlus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full schtasks cmdline and the task action/trigger; confirm the action points to pythonw.exe or a %LocalAppData%\Temp path rather than a signed vendor binary. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and kill the associated pythonw/loader process. 3) Hunt: correlate to the upstream rundll32 WebDAV load and RunMRU paste, and check other hosts for identically-named 'Autoupdate'+8-digit tasks pointing into Temp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("schtasks", "/tn", "Autoupdate")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex "[0-9]{8}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("/tn", "Autoupdate")
| where CommandLine matches regex "[0-9]{8}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

pythonw.exe loader executing from deceptive %LocalAppData%\Temp dir (ACR Stealer) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the ACR Stealer campaign-1 install step where a ZIP payload is extracted into a deceptive folder under %LocalAppData%\Temp (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) and a bundled pythonw.exe is launched from that path by a PowerShell/cmd parent to run the obfuscated Python stealer loader with no console window. Rationale: Anchors on the article's install behavior: a bundled pythonw.exe run from a deceptive %LocalAppData%\Temp dir (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) by a script-interpreter parent; console-less Python from Temp is atypical for legitimate deployed software. Cross-checked against: • https://socfortress.medium.com/acr-stealer-evolution-of-intrusion-chains-and-threat-activity-0052fb3dcc59
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1036.005 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PyInstaller-style apps or dev tooling that unpack an embedded Python into a Temp dir
  • CI/build agents invoking pythonw from a temp working directory
  • Vendor telemetry agents bundling their own Python runtime under LocalAppData
  • Data-science users running notebook helpers from Temp
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "IEX", "DownloadString", "FromBase64String", "Expand-Archive")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the pythonw folder path and sibling files; look for an archive/installer masquerade, a bundled interpreter, and whether the parent PowerShell was the obfuscated loader. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill pythonw and any injected system process, and quarantine the Temp deceptive directory. 3) Hunt: check for VirtualAlloc/Fiber-API in-memory injection, DPAPI browser-store access, and the 'Autoupdate' scheduled task on the same and neighboring hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pythonw.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint traffic to ACR Stealer C2 / dead-drop domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections or DNS lookups to the corroborated ACR Stealer campaign infrastructure (creativecommunityinfo.art, enhanceblabber.cc, sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net, looksta.icu, claude-desktop.gitlab.io) used for WebDAV payload staging and C2 resolution. Rationale: Pre-extracted campaign domains, with sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net independently confirmed as the WebDAV staging host in external write-ups; direct IOC hits on these domains are high-fidelity for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4198788/new-acr-stealer-campaigns-use-webdav-mshta-to-evade-detection.html • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/acr-stealer-clickfix-attacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed crawler or sandbox in the environment resolving the IOC domains
  • Security researcher browsing the C2 domains from a corp host
  • Proxy/DNS logging replayed during IR that re-surfaces historical lookups
  • Domain sinkhole/monitoring service inside the org
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection/lookup (rundll32, pythonw, mshta, powershell) and confirm it is not a known security tool. 2) Contain: block all five domains at DNS+proxy, isolate any host that resolved them, and capture memory before reimage. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to the full ACR chain (RunMRU paste, WebDAV rundll32 load, Autoupdate task, browser-credential access) and check for stolen-token reuse in Entra/M365 sign-in logs.

| where DnsQuery has_any (acrDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)

                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed Pheditor admin editor (pheditor.php) reachable over HTTP AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces any web request to pheditor.php, the single-file admin editor that ships with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579). Because there is no forced password change, any internet-reachable pheditor.php is effectively an unauthenticated RCE endpoint, so simply locating exposed instances is the highest-leverage first pivot. Rationale: Keys on the literal endpoint path pheditor.php confirmed in the advisory and in the live repo source. Defender AH has no web-access-log table so defender_kql is empty; on Apache/nginx front ends substitute CommonSecurityLog.RequestURL for W3CIISLog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php • https://osv.dev/list
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer/sysadmin using Pheditor as an intended file editor
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing for pheditor.php
  • Uptime/monitoring checks hitting the admin path
  • Search-engine or asset-inventory crawlers indexing the web root
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves pheditor.php and whether it is internet-reachable; check the source IPs and user-agents hitting it for scanner vs. human patterns. Step 2 (contain): If exposed to untrusted networks, block the path at the WAF/reverse proxy, take the editor offline, and change the admin password off the default. Step 3 (hunt): Review UC for POST volume (spray), action=terminal requests, php spawning shells, and newly-written .php files on the same host to establish whether default creds were already used.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php"
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| order by Requests desc

description: Detects web requests to pheditor.php, the single-file PHP admin editor shipping with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1595.002
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/pheditor.php'
  condition: selection
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status, Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status, Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Repeated authentication POSTs to Pheditor (default-credential guessing / spray) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a source IP sending many POST requests to pheditor.php in a short window — the shape of default-credential guessing against an instance that ships with password 'admin' and enforces no lockout, expiry, or forced change (CVE-2026-55579). Note: Pheditor returns HTTP 200 for BOTH success and failure, so this pivots on request volume rather than status code. Rationale: Because the app returns 200 on both correct and incorrect passwords (body 'The entry password is not correct.' on failure), a status-code 401->200 rule cannot work here; volume of POSTs to the single login endpoint is the reliable brute/spray signal. Threshold is commented and tunable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin repeatedly re-saving files (each POST hits pheditor.php)
  • Automated CI/CD or backup script interacting with the editor
  • A misconfigured session causing repeated re-login prompts
  • Load-balancer health checks POSTing to the app root
Suppression filter
| search NOT src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the offending source IP's full request sequence; distinguish an admin doing many file saves (varied actions) from monotonic login attempts (repeated pheditor_password submissions). Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF, force the admin password off 'admin', and invalidate active sessions. Step 3 (hunt): If any request in the burst was followed by action=terminal or upload-file activity, treat as compromise and pivot to endpoint UCs (php spawning shell / webshell writes).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php" and csMethod == "POST"
| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| where Attempts >= 10   // 10 = single-user admin editor should see one login POST per session; 10 POSTs/hr from one IP is abnormal
| order by Attempts desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
Pheditor terminal RCE invocation via HTTP (action=terminal / command=) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to pheditor.php carrying the terminal action and command parameter — the built-in terminal feature that yields immediate RCE once the default 'admin' password is used (CVE-2026-55579, and the related command-sanitization bypass CVE-2026-55578). Requires a WAF/proxy that logs query string and/or request body. Rationale: action=terminal and the command parameter are the exact terminal-feature strings confirmed from the Pheditor source. These params are POST body so detection requires WAF/proxy body or query logging; pair with the endpoint UC (php spawning shell) for confirmation where body capture is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Pheditor terminal for routine server tasks
  • Internal automation invoking the terminal action
  • Security testers validating the CVE in a sanctioned pentest
  • WAF false-parsing another app's 'command=' parameter (scope by pheditor.php path mitigates)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the decoded command string from RequestContext/body and the source IP; determine if the caller is a known admin from an expected network. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognized, isolate the web host, kill live php/shell child processes, block the source IP, and rotate the admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to endpoint telemetry for php->sh/bash execution and any newly-dropped .php files; review outbound connections from the web-server user for C2 or data staging.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
| where RequestURL has "action=terminal" or RequestContext has "action=terminal" or RequestURL has "command=" or RequestContext has "command="
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (Pheditor terminal RCE on host) AIExploitation High
Highest-fidelity confirmation of Pheditor terminal RCE: a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php, php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd, w3wp) spawning an interactive shell or recon binary under the web-server account. This is the on-host footprint of the action=terminal command execution described in CVE-2026-55579 / CVE-2026-55578. Rationale: A file-editor's web process spawning /bin/sh + recon commands under www-data/apache is the deterministic on-host signature of the pheditor terminal feature; parent set covers php-fpm, mod_php (apache2/httpd) and IIS FastCGI (php-cgi.exe under w3wp). Datadog covers the Windows FastCGI case; Linux auditd lacks a clean parent field. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PHP application legitimately shelling out (image thumbnailing via ImageMagick, git hooks, cron wrappers)
  • Deployment scripts run as the web-server user
  • Monitoring agents executing whoami/uname under the app account
  • Composer/artisan style tooling invoked by php-fpm
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ffmpeg","git ","composer"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child process command line and full process tree; benign PHP shell-outs are narrow (e.g. convert, git), whereas RCE shows id/whoami/curl or an interactive shell. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, suspend the php-fpm/apache worker, capture volatile memory, and block any C2 IPs seen from the web account. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate .php/.phtml files written by the web process (webshell drop), review pheditor.php modification time, and correlate with inbound action=terminal requests in web/WAF logs.

Web-server/PHP process writing new PHP webshell to web root AIInstallation Medium
Detects a PHP/web-server process creating a new .php/.phtml/.phar file — the on-host result of abusing Pheditor's file-upload (action=upload-file) or file-write editor features to drop a webshell after authenticating with the default password (CVE-2026-55579). Excludes pheditor.php itself (covered separately). Rationale: Pheditor's upload-file action and file editor let an authenticated (default-cred) attacker write arbitrary files; a web process creating new executable PHP content in the web root is the classic webshell-drop signature. Self-file pheditor.php excluded to route those to the dedicated modification UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate deployments/CMS updates writing PHP cache or compiled templates (Twig/Blade cache) under the web user
  • Composer installing PHP packages into the web root
  • A developer legitimately using Pheditor to create new PHP files
  • Plugin/theme installers extracting .php archives
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "cache" and FolderPath !has "vendor" and FolderPath !has "storage/framework"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the newly-written file — template/cache artifacts are auto-generated and predictable, whereas a webshell contains eval/system/base64_decode/assert or request-parameter passthrough. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate the Pheditor admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Search web/WAF logs for subsequent GET/POST requests to the new file path, and check for php spawning shells and outbound C2 from the web account.

| where FileName !~ "pheditor.php"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Modification of Pheditor source file (pheditor.php) — hardcoded hash tamper AIInstallation Medium
Monitors writes/renames to pheditor.php itself. The advisory notes the SHA-512 default-password hash is stored at pheditor.php:11 and the in-app password change rewrites the hash directly into the source file — so any modification is either a legitimate credential change, a hardening action, or attacker persistence editing the admin hash. Flags changes lacking a change-control ticket. Rationale: The advisory explicitly states the SHA-512 hash lives at pheditor.php:11 and the password-change feature writes the new hash back into the source file; FIM on this exact filename catches both legitimate hardening (default hash replaced) and malicious hash swaps for persistent admin access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1554 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin changing the Pheditor password via the app (rewrites the hash by design)
  • Scheduled deployment/git pull updating the file to a patched version (2.0.6+)
  • Sysadmin manually editing the file to remove the default hash (hardening)
  • Backup/restore operations touching the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and user — an in-app change is written by php-fpm/apache, whereas an editor (vim/nano/notepad) or unexpected account is worth scrutiny; confirm against change-control records. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, capture the pre-change hash from backups, restore a known-good pheditor.php, and force a fresh non-default password. Step 3 (hunt): Diff the modified file for an injected/attacker-controlled hash or added PHP, and correlate with prior action=terminal / webshell activity on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua with double-slash path traversal to secrets (CVE-2026-53713) AIExploitation High
Hunts EnvoyExtensionPolicy create/update whose inline Lua contains the exact double-slash bypass paths (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) that defeat the is_critical_path check in security.lua. This is the concrete exploit signature for arbitrary file read from the Envoy Gateway controller pod during Strict validation. Rationale: Uses the exact double-slash payload paths named in the advisory (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) scoped to the envoyextensionpolicies resource — legitimate Lua policies never reference these. Cross-checked GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f and the related GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/CVE-2026-22771/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team submitting a sanctioned validation/PoC policy to confirm patch status
  • Automated CVE-scanner or admission-controller test harness replaying the exploit manifest
  • A Lua policy that legitimately references /certs/ (single slash) mis-typed with a double slash by an operator
  • Backup/GitOps replay re-applying an old exploit manifest already stored in the repo
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !in ("system:serviceaccount:security-tools:cve-scanner") and UserAgent !has "validation-harness"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full requestObject for the flagged EnvoyExtensionPolicy and identify the submitting user/SA, source IP and userAgent; confirm the Lua references the double-slash sensitive paths. 2) Contain: delete the policy, rotate the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount token and any TLS keys reachable from the controller pod, and revoke the submitter's RBAC to create EnvoyExtensionPolicy. 3) Hunt: check the resource status/response for leaked token or file contents (see companion UC), and review kube audit for the envoy-gateway SA being used from unexpected sources afterward.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("//etc/passwd","//var/run/secrets","//proc/self/environ","//certs/")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), SrcIPs = tostring(User.extra)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| table _time, user.username, verb, requestURI, sourceIPs{}, userAgent, objectRef.name, responseStatus.code
| sort - _time
Leaked SA token / file contents in EnvoyExtensionPolicy status (CVE-2026-53713 disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual secret disclosure: an envoyextensionpolicies audit record whose responseObject/status contains a JWT (service-account token), /etc/passwd content, or a PEM private key returned by the failed Strict validation. This confirms exploitation succeeded rather than just being attempted. Rationale: The related advisory confirms the SA token is 'returned in an error which will be displayed in the resource status'; eyJhbGciOi is the constant base64 prefix of a JWT header and root:x:0:0 is the invariant first line of /etc/passwd — both are high-fidelity content markers requiring RequestResponse-level audit. Cross-checked GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A policy legitimately referencing a JWT sample string in a comment (rare)
  • Audit policy not set to RequestResponse level so responseObject is empty (false negative, not FP)
  • Security testing that intentionally reproduces the disclosure in a lab cluster
  • A PEM string embedded in an unrelated but co-located config field captured in the same response
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked material from responseObject — decode the JWT to identify which ServiceAccount was disclosed and its namespace/audience. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/delete that ServiceAccount token (delete the SA's token secret / bounce the pod to force projection refresh) and rotate any disclosed TLS private keys; treat the token as compromised. 3) Hunt: search kube audit for that SA's token being replayed (new sourceIPs, verbs it does not normally perform) and pivot to the companion token-reuse UC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend RespStr = tostring(ResponseObject), StatusStr = tostring(ResponseStatus)
| where RespStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN PRIVATE KEY","serviceaccount/token") or StatusStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, ResponseStatus, RespStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua invoking os/io/debug file primitives AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for EnvoyExtensionPolicy manifests whose inline Lua calls filesystem/OS primitives (io.open, io.popen, os.getenv, os.execute, os.remove, debug.getinfo) — the building blocks any variant of this exploit needs to read the controller pod's files, catching payloads that use paths other than the four named in the advisory. Rationale: Reading a file from Lua requires io/os primitives; legitimate Envoy request-processing Lua manipulates headers/bodies and rarely touches io.open/os.execute, so their presence in a submitted policy is a strong pre-execution signal even when the payload uses a novel path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate advanced Lua filter that reads a mounted config file via io.open
  • os.getenv used to read a benign env var for routing logic
  • Developer testing a Lua snippet copied from a tutorial that includes os.time/os.date near os.execute
  • Vendor-provided policy template that legitimately uses debug for logging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Lua body from requestObject and determine whether the io/os call targets sensitive paths or is benign routing logic. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the policy and rotate controller credentials; if the cluster runs a vulnerable version, prioritise upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to the double-slash and status-disclosure UCs for the same policy name and submitter.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("io.open","io.popen","os.getenv","os.execute","os.remove","debug.getinfo")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous EnvoyExtensionPolicy submitter / suspicious policy name AIDelivery Medium
Profiles who creates EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources to surface rare submitters, and flags policy names containing exploit markers (poc, test, bypass, exploit, passwd). Because the exploit requires an attacker to create/patch the policy via the K8s API, unusual submitters are a leading indicator. Rationale: EnvoyExtensionPolicy objects are normally authored by a small, stable set of platform/GitOps identities; the summarize-by-submitter surfaces rare creators without a hard-coded allowlist, and the name markers catch dropped PoC manifests. Grouping/rarity is evaluated at rule level for Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux SA) creating policies — high count, benign
  • A developer genuinely naming a policy 'canary-test' or 'lua-test'
  • First-time onboarding of a new platform engineer who legitimately creates a policy
  • CI pipeline SA applying policies from a new namespace
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for any rare submitter or exploit-marker name, retrieve the policy body and check for Lua io/os calls or double-slash paths. 2) Contain: if the submitter is unexpected, revoke their create/patch RBAC on envoyextensionpolicies and delete the policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the submitter identity across other CRDs and namespaces for further unauthorized changes.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), PolicyName = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| extend SuspiciousName = PolicyName has_any ("poc","test","bypass","exploit","passwd")
| summarize Count=count(), Policies=make_set(PolicyName, 25), AnySuspicious=max(tolong(SuspiciousName)), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SubmitUser, UserAgent
| order by Count asc

Vulnerable Envoy Gateway version exposed to CVE-2026-53713 AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt that flags hosts/images running an Envoy Gateway version affected by CVE-2026-53713 (>=1.8.0-rc.0 <1.8.1, or <1.7.4) so the exploitable surface is remediated to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 before an attacker submits a malicious EnvoyExtensionPolicy. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the affected/fixed version ranges from the advisory (fixed >=1.7.4 and >=1.8.1). This is the only pivot expressible on Defender/Sentinel native telemetry since the attack itself lives in K8s audit logs; relies on container/software vuln assessment picking up the envoyproxy/gateway package. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched version mis-fingerprinted by TVM as vulnerable (stale scan)
  • An image tag pinned to a fixed digest but labelled with an old version string
  • Non-production/lab Envoy Gateway flagged alongside prod
  • TVM not yet ingesting the CVE definition (false negative, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.7.4 or in 1.8.0-rc.0..1.8.1 and that the instance accepts EnvoyExtensionPolicy submissions. 2) Contain: restrict RBAC so only trusted identities can create/patch EnvoyExtensionPolicy, and apply the Lua-docs Warning-section workarounds until patched. 3) Hunt: upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 and retro-scan kube audit for prior exploit attempts against the affected cluster.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Envoy Gateway ServiceAccount token reuse for anomalous K8s API actions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation hunt: the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway) performing actions it never legitimately performs — creating/deleting pods, exec/attach into pods, reading kube-system secrets, or touching cluster RBAC — which indicates the disclosed token is being replayed against the API server. Rationale: The advisory states the disclosed token can be used to 'read sensitive information from the K8s API Server'; the envoy-gateway controller SA legitimately manages EnvoyProxy infra in its own namespace but never execs into pods, reads kube-system secrets, or edits cluster RBAC — so those verbs under that identity are strong reuse signals. SA name/namespace confirmed from Envoy Gateway deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/operations/deployment-mode/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Envoy Gateway upgrade/migration job temporarily granting the SA broader RBAC
  • A future controller version that legitimately reads a secret in a shared namespace
  • Cluster admin impersonating the SA for troubleshooting (kubectl --as)
  • Backup tooling running under the same SA reading secrets broadly
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "envoy-gateway/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit compare sourceIPs and userAgent against the controller pod's normal client (in-cluster pod IP, controller userAgent); an external IP or kubectl/curl userAgent is high-confidence token theft. 2) Contain: rotate the envoy-gateway SA token immediately, cordon/quarantine any pods created by the SA, and review/revert RBAC changes. 3) Hunt: enumerate every action taken by the token since the disclosure event and check for new workloads, exfil connections, or additional credential reads.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), NS = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where SubmitUser == "system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway"
| where (Verb in ("create","delete") and Resource in ("pods","pods/exec","pods/attach"))
     or (Resource == "secrets" and NS == "kube-system")
     or (Resource in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings","clusterroles"))
| project TimeGenerated, SubmitUser, Verb, Resource, NS, ObjName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53713")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53713")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm installer spawns Python or script host (UAT-11795 Starland RAT) · [LLM] ClickFix mshta.exe silently executing remote HTA then dropping batch (UAT-11795 initial access) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PowerShell AMSI/ETW bypass reflection (UAT-11795 WLDR evasion) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Begun, the Patch Wars have
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] In-memory WLDR PowerShell C2 implant (fileless, no -File, unusual parent) · [LLM] Blockchain-anchored C2 fallback: non-browser process contacting polygon-rpc.com · [LLM] Connection to known UAT-11795 Starland RAT C2 / distribution domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CastleStealer/Starland RAT accessing browser credential stores and crypto wallets · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Trojanized WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm installer spawns Python or script host (UAT-11795 Starland RAT) AIDelivery High
Hunts UAT-11795's supply-chain delivery where a trojanized installer for WebEx, Zoom, MobaXterm, DBeaver or FaceIT spawns a Python interpreter or scripting/LOLBin child that stages the Starland RAT. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact legitimate-tool installer names abused by this campaign paired with anomalous child processes those installers never legitimately launch. Rationale: Anchors on the exact trojanized-installer set (WebEx/Zoom/MobaXterm/DBeaver/FaceIT confirmed across BleepingComputer, SecurityAffairs, gbhackers) as parent, paired with python/script-host children that these GUI installers never legitimately spawn — a two-predicate combination, not a bare process filter. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html

  • Zoom/WebEx auto-update helpers invoking cmd.exe for cleanup
  • IT packaging/repackaging of these installers via a wrapper that launches PowerShell
  • Security testing / EDR validation replaying installer-spawn behavior
  • A developer manually launching python from a terminal that was itself spawned by DBeaver
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/c update","autoupdate","uninstall"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the child command line and SHA256; confirm whether the installer parent came from an official domain/signed publisher and whether the python/script child references a temp path, HTA, or base64 blob. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the python/script process tree, and quarantine the installer binary and any dropped .bat/.hta/.py artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same installer SHA256 across the fleet, look for follow-on mshta.exe, in-memory PowerShell (WLDR), and outbound connections to the campaign C2 domains and polygon-rpc.com.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")

ClickFix mshta.exe silently executing remote HTA then dropping batch (UAT-11795 initial access) AIDelivery High
Hunts the UAT-11795 ClickFix lure where the victim pastes a command that runs mshta.exe against a remote/HTA payload, which silently drops a Windows batch file and the trojanized installer. Article-specific because it targets mshta.exe launched from a user-shell parent (explorer/cmd) with a URL or scriptlet argument — the exact behavior Talos told defenders to monitor. Rationale: Talos explicitly advised monitoring mshta.exe execution and ClickFix; corroborating write-ups describe the HTA being run silently to drop a batch file and trojanized installer, so mshta with a URL/scriptlet arg or a user-shell parent is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Talos explicitly names AMSI and ETW bypasses as UAT-11795 tradecraft; the reflection strings (AmsiUtils/amsiInitFailed/EtwEventWrite) are the canonical, high-signal artifacts of that tampering visible in command lines and AMSI script capture.
