In-memory WLDR PowerShell C2 implant (fileless, no -File, unusual parent) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts UAT-11795's WLDR agent: a fileless PowerShell C2 that runs entirely in memory with a Runspace execution engine. Detects powershell.exe launched with -NoProfile/-NonInteractive/-w hidden but WITHOUT a -File or .ps1 reference, spawned by a non-standard parent (python/mshta/installer), indicating memory-resident script rather than a saved script. Rationale: Talos/corroborators describe WLDR as a fileless PowerShell memory implant with a Runspace engine; the discriminator is hidden/non-interactive PowerShell with NO -File/.ps1 (nothing on disk) spawned by the RAT's Python or the delivery LOLBins — expressed as a leftanti-style negative predicate rather than a bare PS filter. Correlation/negation shape, so Sigma omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-russian-speaking-threat-actor-uat-11795-targets-us-and-europe-with-novel-malware

Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and capture a memory image before reboot (the implant is memory-only). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with encrypted beaconing, DNS to polygon-rpc.com and campaign C2 domains, and prior AMSI/ETW tampering on the same host/session.

Hunts UAT-11795's blockchain-anchored C2 fallback where the implant queries a Polygon RPC endpoint (polygon-rpc.com) to retrieve/refresh its C2 configuration. Detects connections/DNS to polygon-rpc.com and other blockchain RPC/explorer domains initiated by non-browser, non-wallet processes (powershell/python/mshta), which is anomalous for those binaries. Rationale: polygon-rpc.com is a confirmed campaign IOC and the Polygon RPC endpoint the article's blockchain-anchored fallback would query; scoping to non-browser/non-wallet initiating processes removes legitimate crypto-app traffic and makes the RPC contact high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html

Step 3 (hunt): Pull the retrieved payload/response, and hunt the same host for WLDR in-memory PowerShell, AMSI tampering, and the campaign C2 domains.

Connection to known UAT-11795 Starland RAT C2 / distribution domains AICommand & Control High
High-fidelity IOC-match detection for direct connections or DNS resolutions to the UAT-11795 campaign infrastructure disclosed by Talos (eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com, zynaris.io, windowscreenrepairnearme.com, aipythondevs.com). Any endpoint or gateway contact with these domains warrants immediate investigation. Rationale: These six domains are the Talos-disclosed UAT-11795 infrastructure from the pre-extracted IOC set; a direct IOC match on DNS/network telemetry is inherently high-fidelity and needs no behavioral context. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A pre-registered but now-sinkholed domain resolving to a research sinkhole IP
  • Threat-intel/EDR product itself resolving the domain for enrichment
  • An analyst manually browsing the domain during investigation
  • A domain later re-registered by a benign owner after takedown
  • URL-scanning services in the environment pre-fetching the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and host; determine whether the resolution was a real payload fetch vs. a scanner/sinkhole. Step 2 (contain): Block all six domains at DNS/proxy, isolate any host with a non-scanner process making the request. Step 3 (hunt): On confirmed hosts, hunt for the trojanized installer, mshta HTA chain, WLDR PowerShell, CastleStealer wallet access, and Remcos artifacts.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (c2Domains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CastleStealer/Starland RAT accessing browser credential stores and crypto wallets AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the UAT-11795 collection stage where CastleStealer/Starland RAT (running under python.exe or the injected chain) reads browser Login Data / cookie DBs and cryptocurrency wallet files (wallet.dat, keystore) plus Discord/Telegram/Steam session data. Detects non-browser processes touching these sensitive stores. Rationale: Corroborators confirm CastleStealer/Starland RAT targets browser Login Data, 40+ crypto wallets (wallet.dat/keystore/Exodus), and Discord/Telegram/Steam sessions; scoping the access to python/script-host processes (not the browsers themselves) makes credential-store reads high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser backup/sync utilities written in Python reading Login Data
  • Password-manager import tools accessing logins.json
  • Legitimate wallet backup scripts touching wallet.dat
  • EDR/DLP agents enumerating these paths for inventory
  • A developer debugging a Chromium profile with a python script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the accessing process is not a sanctioned backup/sync tool; capture its parent chain (installer → python → collection). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, force-reset credentials for browsers/accounts stored on it, and move any crypto wallet assets to a clean device. Step 3 (hunt): Look for exfil to campaign C2 domains, staged archives (zip/7z) in temp, and parallel Remcos RAT indicators on the same or peer hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\", "Login Data", @"\Network\Cookies", "logins.json", "wallet.dat", @"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Exodus\", @"\discord\Local Storage\", @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","mshta.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\", "Login Data", @"\Network\Cookies", "logins.json", "wallet.dat", @"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Exodus\", @"\discord\Local Storage\", @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata\")
| where tolower(ActingProcessName) has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","mshta.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-56155", "CVE-2026-56164", "CVE-2026-50661")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "b8be9a5e0a191050f9099c11c155b436863e9bc43bc904cdb842e249679aa35a", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a", "0398df5a18f71efcfeef4571a2cef577"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Begun, the Patch Wars have Exploitation High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Begun, the Patch Wars have
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

HelloNet DLL side-load: wtsapi32.dll dropped into ViPNet Update System directory AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a wtsapi32.dll (or any DLL) inside C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System, the folder abused by the HelloInjector loader for DLL sideloading against itcsrvup64.exe. wtsapi32.dll is a genuine System32 API-set DLL, so a copy landing in a vendor update directory is highly anomalous. Rationale: Anchors on the exact abused path 'C:\Program Files (x86)\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System' and the sideloaded DLL name wtsapi32.dll from the article; wtsapi32.dll is a legit System32 module so a copy in a vendor directory is near-zero-FP.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1195.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate InfoTeCS ViPNet product update dropping a genuinely signed DLL during an official patch cycle
  • InfoTeCS installer/MSI repair operations writing bundled DLLs
  • Security tooling (backup/AV) staging a copy of a DLL into the folder during scanning
  • Admin manually copying a diagnostic DLL into the directory for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "InfoTeCS" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("itcsrvup64.exe","itcupdate.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of the new DLL and its InitiatingProcess; check signer — legitimate ViPNet DLLs are InfoTeCS-signed. wtsapi32.dll here should be unsigned/untrusted. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill itcsrvup64.exe and any svchost.exe it spawned, quarantine the DLL. 3) Hunt: search for C:\Users\Public\tesh4RPC.txt, frontpage.exe under C:\Users\Public\Music, and outbound connections to 5.39.253.206/176.32.34.135 across the estate.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\InfoTeCS\VIPNet Update System"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloInjector: itcsrvup64.exe loads unexpected wtsapi32.dll from ViPNet directory AIInstallation High
Detects the ViPNet update executable itcsrvup64.exe loading wtsapi32.dll from its own program directory instead of System32 — the runtime signature of the HelloInjector DLL side-load persistence. Startup execution of itcsrvup64.exe pulls in the attacker DLL. Rationale: Uses the article's named loader executable itcsrvup64.exe and the exact side-loaded module wtsapi32.dll; genuine wtsapi32.dll always resolves from System32, so a load from the ViPNet path is definitive of the sideload. Sentinel left empty — no clean image-load table in this tenant's schema.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1547.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A future legitimate ViPNet build shipping its own wtsapi32.dll dependency in-directory
  • DLL redirection / SxS manifest testing by InfoTeCS support
  • Application virtualization layer (e.g. App-V) redirecting module paths
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded wtsapi32.dll SHA256 differs from the Microsoft System32 build and is unsigned. 2) Contain: stop the ViPNet Update System service, isolate host, quarantine the DLL. 3) Hunt: inspect svchost.exe (netsvcs) memory injection artifacts and the tesh4RPC.txt proxy log on the same host.

| where FolderPath !contains @"\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !contains @"\Windows\SysWOW64"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc

HelloInjector code injection into svchost.exe netsvcs from ViPNet-loaded module AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces svchost.exe (netsvcs host) loading a module out of the InfoTeCS ViPNet Update System directory — the injection footprint left when HelloInjector uses NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx to run HelloProxy inside a svchost hosting netsvcs. Normal svchost never loads modules from a vendor update folder. Rationale: Combines the article's injection target (svchost hosting netsvcs) with the ViPNet directory path the malicious module lives in; svchost loading from a third-party update folder is a strong injection tell. Sentinel empty — no image-load table available.
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1055
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet service legitimately hosted under svchost loading its own signed helper DLL
  • Endpoint security agent injecting a monitoring DLL into svchost
  • Windows servicing operation temporarily mapping a vendor module
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in~ (dynamic([])) )
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the svchost PID's loaded modules and network sockets; confirm listeners on ports 5003/5060 (HelloProxy). 2) Contain: suspend/kill the injected svchost, isolate host. 3) Hunt: pivot to itcsrvup64.exe sideload on the same host and outbound sessions to 5.39.253.206.

HelloProxy artifact: tesh4RPC.txt written under C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Hunts creation of the file C:\Users\Public\tesh4RPC.txt — the log HelloProxy writes for every AFD_RECV socket event (threadid:<TID> pid=<PID>). This filename is unique to this campaign and is a near-certain compromise indicator. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt is a verbatim, campaign-unique filename from the article's HelloProxy description; there is no benign software that writes this file, making it an alert-grade IOC.
ATT&CKT1090 T1071
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Effectively none — filename is campaign-unique
  • Analyst copying the IOC file onto a test host during investigation
  • Threat-intel/IOC synchronization tooling staging sample artifacts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (should be an injected svchost.exe); read the file — entries are threadid/pid pairs proving active proxy sessions. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the proxy svchost, block 5.39.253.206/176.32.34.135 at the firewall. 3) Hunt: check for listeners on 5003/5060 and for the frontpage.exe reverse SSH tunnel campaign-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel from C:\Users\Public\Music to HelloNet C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects the campaign's data-tunnel technique: a renamed PuTTY binary (frontpage.exe) launched from C:\Users\Public\Music with a reverse-tunnel command line (-N -R) to sftp@5.39.253.206 on port 3522. Catches both the exact IOC and the generic renamed-PuTTY-reverse-tunnel shape. Rationale: Uses the article's exact tunnel IOCs — folder C:\Users\Public\Music, the renamed PuTTY binary, the -N -R reverse-tunnel flags, and C2 IP 5.39.253.206 — while also catching the renamed-PuTTY variant via product-name metadata.
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1571
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using PuTTY/plink for a reverse tunnel to an authorized jump host (not to 5.39.253.206)
  • Developer SSH remote-forward for local service testing
  • Backup software invoking sftp with an -R argument coincidentally
  • Media apps legitimately running from Public\Music (won't match the -N -R SSH shape)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "-R " and not (ProcessCommandLine has "5.39.253.206" or FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm destination IP/port — 5.39.253.206:3522 is the C2; inspect the -R forward target and captured -pw. 2) Contain: kill the tunnel process, block 5.39.253.206 egress, rotate any credentials exposed on the tunnel command line. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts with binaries under C:\Users\Public\Music and PuTTY-metadata processes making outbound SSH.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "5.39.253.206")
     or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R " and ProcessCommandLine has "-N")
     or (ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "PuTTY" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R " and FileName !~ "putty.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "5.39.253.206")
     or (NewProcessName has @"\Users\Public\Music" and CommandLine has "-R " and CommandLine has "-N")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloExecutor reconnaissance: enumeration of ViPNet key-material export directories AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the HelloExecutor recon pattern of listing InfoTeCS/ViPNet Administrator and Client export folders (kc\Export, ViPNet Client\Export) — where ViPNet key containers live. Targeting these specific directories is a strong campaign-specific discovery signal distinct from generic host enumeration. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim recon targets — the InfoTeCS ViPNet Administrator and Client Export/kc\Export directories that store ViPNet key material — which is far more specific than the generic 'net user /net group' recon also listed.
ATT&CKT1083 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ViPNet administrator legitimately listing export folders during key distribution operations
  • Backup jobs enumerating the InfoTeCS directory tree
  • Software inventory/asset scanners walking Program Files
  • Helpdesk troubleshooting ViPNet client configuration
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and AccountName in~ ("viadmin","vipnetadmin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify parent process — a svchost.exe or non-interactive parent issuing these dir commands is suspicious vs an admin cmd session. 2) Contain: if parent is injected svchost, isolate host and preserve the ViPNet key export folder for IR. 3) Hunt: correlate with tesh4RPC.txt, itcsrvup64.exe sideload, and outbound tunnels on the same host and other ViPNet-connected machines.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", @"ViPNet Client\Export", @"kc\Export")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "infotecs"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", @"ViPNet Client\Export", @"kc\Export")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Enumeration of ViPNet key-material export directories

description: dir/listing commands targeting InfoTeCS ViPNet Administrator/Client export folders holding key containers — HelloExecutor recon

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | regex("(?i)infotecs", field=CommandLine) | regex("(?i)(ViPNet Administrator|ViPNet Client\\\\Export|kc\\\\Export)", field=CommandLine) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to the HelloNet command-server IPs 5.39.253.206 (SSH tunnel/C2 on ports 5003/3522) and 176.32.34.135. Especially high-fidelity when the initiating process is svchost.exe or a binary under C:\Users\Public\Music. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the two campaign C2 IPs from the article's IOC set; pairing the initiating process (svchost.exe / Public\Music binary) raises confidence and aids triage.
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IP reassigned to benign hosting after the campaign (validate first-seen date)
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation VM deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security scanner probing the IP range
  • Analyst investigation traffic to the C2 from a research host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and port (3522/5003 = SSH tunnel/proxy); confirm the host also shows sideload or tesh4RPC.txt artifacts. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the connecting process. 3) Hunt: sweep firewall/proxy logs for all internal hosts that ever reached either IP and check each for ViPNet update-directory tampering.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound connection to HelloNet ViPNet C2 IPs

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public · [LLM] GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# · [LLM] GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the ThumbcacheService collection database thumbcache_605a.db in C:\Users\Public\, where GoSerpent stages harvested .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx documents before exfiltration. Legitimate Windows thumbnail caches use the same thumbcache_*.db naming but live under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, never in the Public profile, making the Public-path variant article-specific. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim filename thumbcache_605a.db (code block) and the C:\Users\Public\ staging path; legitimate thumbcache DBs never live in the Public profile, so the path variant catches renamed samples with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or admin manually copying their AppData thumbnail cache into C:\Users\Public for troubleshooting
  • Backup/migration tooling that mirrors user profile Explorer caches into a shared Public folder
  • Forensic/IR tools exporting thumbcache artifacts to C:\Users\Public for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the DB; a service DLL host (svchost.exe hosting an unknown service) or a binary in Public/Temp is high-suspicion. Inspect the file for a 7-Zip archive nearby and confirm it is not a genuine Explorer cache. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DB and any adjacent .7z archives for analysis, and disable/stop the suspicious Windows service backing ThumbcacheService. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for 7-Zip archiving with the campaign password, lass.exe/updates.exe processes, and SAM/LSASS credential-dumping activity in the prior days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\" and FileName startswith "thumbcache_" and FileName endswith ".db")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\" and TargetFileName startswith "thumbcache_" and TargetFileName endswith ".db")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ThumbcacheService's 7-Zip archiving stage, which packs collected documents into password-protected archives using the fixed password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# with a 20MB volume limit. The password string is a unique campaign artifact, so any command line containing it is effectively a signature regardless of the archiver binary name. Rationale: The password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# is a verbatim campaign string with effectively zero legitimate use; matching its alphanumeric core (vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6) survives quoting/escaping and catches renamed 7z binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-running the sample's archive command during malware analysis on a lab host
  • Threat-intel/IR playbook that references the password string in a script comment for testing detections
  • Purple-team exercise emulating GoSerpent's archiving stage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the archiver binary (7z.exe/7za.exe or a renamed copy) and the target file set; look for the -v20m volume flag and the source documents being packed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the produced archives, and block outbound to any network share the archives were destined for. 3) Hunt: locate thumbcache_605a.db on the same host, review the credential-dumping activity that supplied the share credentials, and check network-share write events for exfiltration of the archives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of GoSerpent's masquerading binaries lass.exe (mimicking lsass.exe) and updates.exe, which host the SOCKS5 proxy/RAT. lass.exe is never a legitimate Windows binary, and updates.exe running from user-writable/staging directories is a strong anomaly for this campaign. Rationale: lass.exe and updates.exe are named verbatim in the article (code blocks) as GoSerpent's process-masquerading filenames; lass.exe has no legitimate counterpart and the path constraint on updates.exe filters the common legitimate updater binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party application shipping its own updates.exe from ProgramData/AppData (e.g. some auto-updaters)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named lass.exe in a source tree
  • Software packaging or installer temp extraction dropping an updates.exe into a Temp directory
  • Portable app launched from a USB/Public share named updates.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and signer of the process; unsigned lass.exe or a Go-compiled updates.exe from a user-writable path is high-confidence. Check for a listening socket / SOCKS5 behavior and outbound C2 from the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block the associated C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search for ThumbcacheService staging (thumbcache_605a.db), the 7-Zip archive password, and credential-dumping tools deployed by the same backdoor across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "lass.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith @"\lass.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "lass.exe"
    or ((TargetProcessName endswith @"\updates.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "updates.exe") and TargetProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the QuarksDumpLocalHash tool GoSerpent deploys to extract local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive for offline cracking, plus the equivalent reg.exe SAM/SECURITY hive save. This is distinct from LSASS memory access and targets the on-disk SAM credential store. Rationale: Anchored on the named tool QuarksDumpLocalHash and its documented SAM-hive extraction behavior; the reg.exe hive-save branch catches the same TTP if the operator uses a LOLBin instead of the custom tool, and it deliberately avoids overlapping the existing LSASS-access detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting a SAM/SECURITY hive for legitimate password-audit or migration tooling
  • Endpoint hardening/audit software (e.g. compliance scanners) reading local hive backups
  • IR/forensics collection scripts that reg save HKLM\SAM for evidence
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("forensic_collector.exe","psexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a hive save or quarks* binary spawned by an unknown Go backdoor (lass.exe/updates.exe) rather than an admin session is high-confidence. Check whether the resulting hive/hash output was written to a staging path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local account passwords (and any domain accounts used interactively), and revoke cached credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with ThumbcacheService staging and network-share writes — the dumped credentials are used to authenticate to shares for exfiltration; review share-access logs for the affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "quarks" or ProcessCommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "quarks" or CommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and (CommandLine has @"hklm\sam" or CommandLine has @"hklm\security"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash SAM Hive Dump
id: d70e2b19-3c84-4a56-b0f1-9a2c4e7d6b12
description: Detects QuarksDumpLocalHash or reg.exe saving the SAM/SECURITY hive to extract local password hashes, as deployed by the GoSerpent backdoor.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    CommandLine|contains: 'QuarksDumpLocalHash'
  selection_toolname:
    Image|contains: 'quarks'
  selection_regsave:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'save'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hklm\sam'
      - 'hklm\security'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\QuarksDumpLocalHash.exe OR *\quarksdumplocalhash.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*QuarksDumpLocalHash* OR *quarksdumplocalhash*) OR (@Image:(*\reg.exe OR *\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*save* OR *SAVE*) AND @CommandLine:(*HKLM\SAM* OR *hklm\sam* OR *HKLM\SECURITY* OR *hklm\security*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/quarks/i OR CommandLine=/QuarksDumpLocalHash/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\reg\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/save/i AND CommandLine=/hklm\\(sam|security)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UAT-11795 weaponized HTA delivery via mshta.exe from ClickFix staging domain · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] UAT-11795 trojanized installer spawns Python bytecode loader (PythonLauncher-*) · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland RAT HWID C2 beaconing from Python process · [LLM] UAT-11795 staging chain + WLDR PowerShell C2 over /feed/ and /alpha/ paths · [LLM] Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (Eth_call) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Starland RAT browser credential & cryptocurrency wallet harvesting via Python · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
UAT-11795 weaponized HTA delivery via mshta.exe from ClickFix staging domain AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launching a remote/local HTA stager, the article-described entry point for UAT-11795 (weaponized HTA downloader delivered via a likely ClickFix technique from zynaris[.]io). Flags mshta invocations carrying a URL/.hta argument, especially referencing the campaign staging domain, and their child installer/PowerShell spawns. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated entry point (mshta.exe HTA downloader via ClickFix) and the campaign staging domain zynaris[.]io; mshta with a remote/.hta argument is rare in benign user activity, making it high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise apps that still ship .hta admin utilities launched via mshta
  • IT automation/logon scripts invoking mshta with an internal http path
  • Software packaging tools (SCCM/Intune) that stage .hta helpers
  • Developer testing of HTA content locally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\CCM" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the mshta command line and resolve the URL host — confirm whether it is zynaris[.]io or another external/unfamiliar domain vs an internal IT resource. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the staging domain at proxy/DNS, and capture the downloaded HTA/installer from %TEMP% for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for follow-on trojanized installer execution (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FaceIT), python.exe spawns from PythonLauncher-* folders, and outbound to windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com / aipythondevs[.]com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io", ".hta", "http://", "https://", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          MshtaCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has_any ("zynaris.io", ".hta", "http://", "https://", "javascript:", "vbscript:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAT-11795 mshta.exe Remote HTA Stager Execution

UAT-11795 trojanized installer spawns Python bytecode loader (PythonLauncher-*) AIInstallation High
Hunts trojanized software installers (MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, FACEIT) whose NSIS package spawns byte-compiled Python that loads Starland RAT in memory. Anchors on the exact installer filenames from the article and the PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} working folder plus Telegram bot beacon traffic. Rationale: Uses the exact trojanized installer filenames (MobaXterm_v26.1.exe etc.) and the article's PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} loader artifact; a signed-looking installer spawning a Python interpreter is anomalous and campaign-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python-based installers or apps that bundle an embedded interpreter
  • Developer machines where DBeaver/other tools genuinely launch Python plugins
  • Software distribution repackaging that wraps installers and calls python
  • Data-science tooling installers extracting to random temp folders
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the installer file's origin (download URL/referrer) and digital signature; genuine vendor installers are signed and do not spawn python.exe. Capture the PythonLauncher-* folder contents. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the installer and Python artifacts, and block the download source. 3) Hunt: check the host for outbound to api.telegram.org (bots 8384531459 / 7993597060), Starland C2 domains, and CastleStealer/Remcos follow-on shellcode execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe","Zoom installer.exe")
     or ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
     or FolderPath has "PythonLauncher-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          Installer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InstallerCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          PyImage = FolderPath,
          PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
     or CommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT HWID C2 beaconing from Python process AICommand & Control High
Detects Starland RAT command-and-control: a python.exe/pythonw.exe process making outbound connections to the primary Starland C2 domains windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com and aipythondevs[.]com, whose URLs embed a per-victim C: drive volume serial number as the final path component. High-fidelity because a Python interpreter beaconing to these specific domains is not benign. Rationale: Anchors on the two named primary Starland RAT C2 domains and the article's per-victim volume-serial URL scheme, initiated specifically by a Python interpreter — the combination is not observed in benign traffic. Sentinel query uses ImWebSession host/URL fields (no process column exists on that table). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox detonation of the sample generating C2 traffic
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving/curling the IOC domains
  • Proxy prefetch/URL-scanning appliances touching the domain
  • A future benign re-registration of a lapsed hijacked domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Anaconda3\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pip install"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a Python interpreter and extract the full URL — the trailing hex segment is the victim volume serial (unique fingerprint). 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com and aipythondevs[.]com, and kill the python process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the Polygon smart-contract fallback (Eth_call / 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba), staging-domain traffic to eorthopaedics[.]com/sastoro[.]com /feed/ and /alpha/, and browser/wallet file access.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
     or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(windowscreenrepairnearme|aipythondevs)\.com/.+/[0-9A-Fa-f]{8}$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
     or Url has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 staging chain + WLDR PowerShell C2 over /feed/ and /alpha/ paths AICommand & Control High
Detects the UAT-11795 PowerShell stage chain and parallel WLDR C2: PowerShell (or other host) retrieving payloads from eorthopaedics[.]com and sastoro[.]com under the article-specific /feed/ and /alpha/ URL paths that carry HWID-parameterized encrypted envelopes. Targets both the staging download and the persistent WLDR beacon. Rationale: Uses the two named staging/parallel-C2 domains plus the article's distinctive /feed/ and /alpha/ routing paths that carry HWID-encrypted envelopes — the host+path combination is a precise campaign fingerprint that avoids matching the domains' legitimate content. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate visitors to eorthopaedics[.]com (a likely hijacked but otherwise real site) hitting unrelated pages — mitigated by the /feed//alpha/ path requirement
  • Security tooling crawling the domains for IOC validation
  • Proxy URL-rewrite that appends /feed/ style paths
  • RSS/feed readers coincidentally polling a /feed/ path on these hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and inspect the full URL — a hex/HWID trailing component under /feed/ or /alpha/ confirms the WLDR envelope. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block eorthopaedics[.]com and sastoro[.]com, and capture the PowerShell stager from memory/disk. 3) Hunt: look for the WLDR Runspace loader, New-ScheduledTask persistence, and correlate with Starland RAT beacons to windowscreenrepairnearme[.]com / aipythondevs[.]com on the same or related hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com")
| where RemoteUrl has "/feed/" or RemoteUrl has "/alpha/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstHostname in~ ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com") or Url has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com"))
| where Url has "/feed/" or Url has "/alpha/"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
