Starland RAT Polygon smart-contract fallback C2 resolution (Eth_call) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects Starland RAT's resilient fallback channel: retrieval of an XOR-encrypted backup C2 domain from the Polygon smart contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba via a public JSON-RPC Eth_call. Anchors on the exact contract address string and Polygon RPC endpoints appearing in process/script activity or outbound traffic. Rationale: The contract address 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba is a unique, article-specific string; combined with eth_call to Polygon RPC by a python/powershell process it is an unambiguous fallback-C2 indicator. Medium confidence because obfuscation may hide the literal string, so the network-to-Polygon-RPC leg is included. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1102 T1568
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain developers/wallet apps making eth_call to polygon-rpc.com
  • Crypto trading bots or DeFi tooling on the endpoint
  • Node/Python web3 libraries in a dev environment querying Polygon
  • Browser extensions (MetaMask) proxying RPC — though those rarely appear as python/powershell initiators
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process — a python/powershell interpreter querying Polygon RPC or embedding the contract address is not typical business use; check the host for Starland RAT artifacts. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block polygon-rpc.com egress for that process; the fallback resolves the next C2 so also block primary/staging domains. 3) Hunt: decode any XOR-encrypted domain returned and add it to blocklists; sweep the estate for the same contract-address string or eth_call pattern from non-developer hosts.
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba","eth_call","polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com/polygon")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet")
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="Network", FileName=InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=RemoteUrl
)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon-mainnet") or Url has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT browser credential & cryptocurrency wallet harvesting via Python AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Starland RAT / CastleStealer collection stage: a python.exe/pythonw.exe (or PythonLauncher-*) process reading browser profile stores (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Login Data) and cryptocurrency wallet directories. Article states the RAT steals browser data and crypto wallets; corroborating reporting notes 40+ wallet targets. Rationale: Combines the article's stated collection behaviour (browser data + crypto wallets) with the campaign's Python execution vector; requiring a Python interpreter to touch >=2 distinct credential/wallet stores raises fidelity over a generic browser-file-access rule. Wallet target breadth corroborated by external reporting (40+ wallets). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/starland-rat-steals-browser-credentials/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python-based backup/migration scripts copying browser profiles
  • Security tooling or DFIR scripts collecting browser artifacts
  • Developer test automation (Selenium/Playwright) reading browser profiles
  • Password-manager import utilities written in Python touching Login Data
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Anaconda3\\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("selenium","playwright","backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Python process lineage (was it spawned by a trojanized installer / PythonLauncher-*?) and enumerate exactly which browser/wallet stores were read. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset credentials for accounts stored in the affected browsers; advise the user to move any crypto wallet funds from a clean device. 3) Hunt: correlate with Starland C2 beacons and Telegram exfil (bots 8384531459 / 7993597060), and search for CastleStealer .NET stealer or Remcos artifacts as follow-on payloads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "PythonLauncher-"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    @"\User Data\", "Login Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\",
    @"\Exodus\", @"\Ethereum\", @"\Electrum\", "wallet.dat", @"\Bitcoin\", "web3")
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(FolderPath), SamplePaths = make_set(FolderPath, 12), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2   // 2 = require multiple sensitive stores, not a single incidental hit
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") or ActingProcessName has "PythonLauncher-"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\User Data\\", "Login Data", "\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\", "\\Exodus\\", "\\Ethereum\\", "\\Electrum\\", "wallet.dat", "\\Bitcoin\\")
| summarize PathsTouched = dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 12), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE) (@TargetFilename:*\User\ Data\* OR @TargetFilename:*Login\ Data* OR @TargetFilename:*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\* OR @TargetFilename:*\Exodus\* OR @TargetFilename:*\Ethereum\* OR @TargetFilename:*wallet.dat*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\pythonw?\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\User Data\\\\|Login Data|\\\\Mozilla\\\\Firefox\\\\Profiles\\\\|\\\\Exodus\\\\|\\\\Ethereum\\\\|wallet\.dat|\\\\Electrum\\\\)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN (python.exe,pythonw.exe) AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Ethereum\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Exodus\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*wallet*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN (python.exe,pythonw.exe) AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Ethereum\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Exodus\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*wallet*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery

Microsoft Security BlogStepSecurity
2026-07-16 18 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors compromised AsyncAPI packages and weaponized trusted CI/CD workflows to distribute malware through npm. This analysis breaks down the attack chain, payload delivery, and recommended defenses. The post Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload delivery appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache · [LLM] Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload deliv
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory · [LLM] Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for the five backdoored @asyncapi package versions (@asyncapi/specs 6.11.2 & 6.11.2-alpha.1, generator 3.3.1, generator-components 0.7.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1) landing on developer/CI hosts via npm or Yarn dependency resolution. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft/Socket confirmed, not generic 'npm install' activity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft published and Socket/StepSecurity independently confirmed; package name is always lowercase in the registry/cache so no casing enumeration needed, and version+name combined is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or IR teams intentionally downloading the malicious versions into a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory that cached the bad versions during the exposure window and is now being audited
  • Developers who pinned 6.11.2 in a lockfile and re-ran install against a still-poisoned private proxy
  • Yarn/npm cache directories restored from an old backup image containing the version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npm-cli.js") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("malware-analysis","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is a real install target (node_modules, .yarn/cache, npm _cacache) and not a knowingly-collected sample; capture the host, user, and whether it's a dev box or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host, purge npm & Yarn caches, remove all five affected versions, and pin @asyncapi/specs to a known-good release; block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 at egress. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to a detached node child writing sync.js under the NodeJS masquerade dir and any outbound IPFS fetch; rotate every credential reachable from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS, SSH keys).

| where (FileName has "specs" and FileName has "6.11.2")
    or (FileName has "generator-helpers" and FileName has "1.1.1")
    or (FileName has "generator-components" and FileName has "0.7.1")
    or (FileName has "generator" and FileName has "3.3.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

    or (TargetFileName has "generator" and TargetFileName has "3.3.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time loader writing its IPFS-fetched second stage as sync.js into the OS-specific NodeJS masquerade folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS, ~/.config/NodeJS). Article-specific: the fixed filename sync.js plus the fake NodeJS directory is a unique fingerprint of this campaign, not generic file drops. Rationale: Uses the verbatim FILE_NAME='sync.js' constant and the getTargetDirectory() 'NodeJS' masquerade paths from the article's code block 2 — the combination is unique to this loader and confirmed by Microsoft's own Query 1. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that genuinely names its data dir 'NodeJS' and writes a sync.js sync script
  • Developer scaffolding/boilerplate that creates a sync.js worker under an app-support folder
  • A backup/restore of a previously-infected profile re-materializing sync.js
  • Security tooling replaying the sample into a NodeJS folder during analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "npm" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "yarn"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash sync.js and check its parent process — a node.exe/node child with detached/hidden flags confirms; benign scripts have a real signed parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process tree, delete sync.js, and block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 plus ipfs.io retrieval at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot to which @asyncapi version installed on the host, look for outbound IPFS CID fetches (Qmet4… / QmQobZSp…), and rotate all credentials reachable from the environment given Miasma's credential-harvest module.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time payload's execution stage: a node process launching the dropped sync.js out of the NodeJS masquerade directory, matching the spawn('node',[payloadPath],{detached,stdio:ignore,windowsHide}) pattern. Article-specific via the sync.js + NodeJS command-line pairing (mirrors Microsoft's published hunting Query 1). Rationale: Combines the verbatim FILE_NAME 'sync.js' and 'NodeJS' masquerade path from code block 2 with a node interpreter parent — the same signal Microsoft ships as their behavioral coverage for the detached Node.js spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Electron/CLI tooling that stores helper scripts under an app-support NodeJS folder
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
  • A monorepo build task named sync.js executed with a NodeJS-prefixed cwd
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","webpack","vite","--build") and DeviceName has "build")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and grandparent — a build/import node.exe (from npm/yarn) spawning this detached child confirms the chain; note the SHA256 of sync.js. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node tree, remove sync.js, and block the C2 IP/ports and IPFS egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to the affected @asyncapi version on the host and any outbound connection to 85.137.53.71 or ipfs.io CIDs within minutes; force credential rotation for npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH accessible from that host.

Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma runtime's command-and-control beaconing to the hardcoded controller 85.137.53.71 over its three fixed ports. Article-specific: a single named IP plus the exact non-standard port trio Microsoft told orgs to block — near-zero ambiguity. Rationale: Single hardcoded controller IP plus the exact port trio (8080/8081/8091) that Microsoft explicitly recommended blocking — a definitive C2 indicator with essentially no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-attack-delivers-multi-stage-miasma-botnet-via-compromised-github-act • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IR analyst deliberately connecting to the C2 for characterization from a sanctioned sandbox
  • A honeypot or deception host configured to beacon to known-bad IPs
  • Vulnerability scanner probing the IP as part of an external asset sweep
  • Reuse of 85.137.53.71 by an unrelated benign service after takedown (verify recency)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — node.exe/sync.js confirms Miasma; capture host, user, and beacon cadence. 2) Contain: isolate host, block 85.137.53.71 on 8080/8081/8091 at perimeter and host firewall, and kill the responsible process tree. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same IP/ports and for the decentralized fallback channels (Nostr, Ethereum, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p, IPFS); enumerate which imported @asyncapi and rotate every reachable credential.

| order by Timestamp desc

| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| where DstPortNumber in (8080, 8081, 8091)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DstDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) AIDelivery High
Detects the child loader fetching sync.js from IPFS via ipfs.io, keyed on the two campaign CIDs (Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf for specs, QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 for the generator family) or any node process hitting the ipfs.io gateway. Article-specific via the exact IPFS content identifiers. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim IPFS CIDs from the article's Table 2 and the ipfs.io gateway constant from code block 2; a node interpreter fetching from ipfs.io is itself anomalous in most enterprises and the CID match is definitive. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Web3/blockchain developer legitimately pinning or fetching content from ipfs.io via a Node app
  • CI jobs that pull assets from public IPFS gateways
  • Browser-based IPFS usage co-resident on a dev workstation (not node-initiated)
  • Analyst reproducing the fetch of the campaign CIDs in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("web3","blockchain") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ipfs-http-client")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe and whether the URL contains a campaign CID (definitive) vs generic ipfs.io (assess node context). 2) Contain: isolate host, block ipfs.io egress for server/build subnets, kill the node process, and remove any sync.js written afterward. 3) Hunt: correlate the fetch time to a preceding @asyncapi install and a following connection to 85.137.53.71; check other hosts for the same CIDs and rotate credentials exposed to the environment.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any ("Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"))
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName has "node" and RemoteUrl contains "ipfs.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9")
    or Url has "ipfs.io/ipfs/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Malicious @velora-dex/sdk (9.4.1/9.4.2) pulled into GitHub Actions build runner AIDelivery High
Hunts CI/build runners that install the trojanized @velora-dex/sdk npm package — the compromise that dropped a macOS backdoor the moment the SDK was imported. Version 9.4.0 is confirmed clean, so any install of a non-9.4.0 version of this specific package on a runner is suspect. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package name '@velora-dex/sdk' and excludes the confirmed-clean 9.4.0, per Corgea (v9.4.1 published 2026-04-07) and StepSecurity — a named-package/version IOC that only fires on genuinely-affected installs. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally installing the clean 9.4.0 pin (excluded, but a lockfile resolving without an explicit version tag may show no version)
  • Internal mirror/registry proxy re-fetching the package name in log lines during cache warmup
  • Security researchers/DFIR reproducing the compromise in a sandbox runner
  • A vendored monorepo referencing 'velora-dex/sdk' in a path or comment picked up by broad command lines
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0") | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact resolved version from the runner's package-lock.json/npm cache and the workflow run; 9.4.1/9.4.2 = confirmed malicious, 9.4.0 = clean. 2) Contain: isolate the runner (especially macOS/Bitrise hosts), revoke any secrets that were in scope for that job (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, registry/deploy tokens), and rebuild the runner from a clean image. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'C2 beacon to Velora infra (89.36.224.5)' and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same DeviceId, and diff lockfiles across all repos for the pinned bad version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has "velora-dex/sdk@9.4.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Build runner beacon/exfil to Velora backdoor C2 (89.36.224.5 / datahub.ink) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any outbound connection from a runner or endpoint to the confirmed Velora-SDK backdoor C2 infrastructure — IP 89.36.224.5 and domains datahub.ink, cloud-sync.online, byte-io.us. These are where the macOS implant fetched its shell script and exfiltrated harvested signing keys and tokens. Rationale: IP 89.36.224.5 is confirmed as the Velora backdoor C2 by StepSecurity, Corgea and Phoenix Security; the three domains are enumerated verbatim in Corgea's IOC list. Direct-hit IOC match, near-zero legitimate reason for a build host to reach these. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox tooling actively probing the C2 (verify the initiating process is a scanner)
  • A newly-registered legitimate service reusing the 89.36.224.5 host after takedown (re-validate IP ownership)
  • Security team detonating the sample in an authorized lab connected to production telemetry
  • DNS sinkhole or passive-DNS collector resolving the domains for research
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threatintel-scanner.exe","nessus","nmap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the runner (node/npm/curl vs a legit tool) and the direction/volume of traffic to 89.36.224.5. 2) Contain: block the IP and three domains at egress/proxy, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every secret the affected build job could touch (Apple signing certs, provisioning profiles, App Store Connect keys, registry tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate against the @velora-dex/sdk install UC and the launchctl-persistence UC on the same host, and search all runners for prior connections to these indicators.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DstIpAddr, Detail = Url),
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has_any ("datahub.ink","cloud-sync.online","byte-io.us") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery, Detail = DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velora macOS backdoor launchctl persistence (com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the persistence artifacts the Velora SDK backdoor installs on macOS build runners: a masquerading LaunchAgent plist and support directory impersonating Apple's Terminal, plus the known payload hashes. Fires on the exact plist name, path, or file hash written to a runner. Rationale: com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist and the ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.Terminal/profiler directory are the exact persistence artifacts documented by Corgea; the plist name masquerades as Apple's Terminal but is not a genuine Apple file, so any write is high-fidelity. Payload SHA256s are the article-supplied IOCs, kept alongside the corroborated path artifacts. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://opensourcemalware.com/blog/velora-hacked • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine Apple/Terminal update writing legitimately-named plists (the profiler variant is not a real Apple file, so overlap is unlikely)
  • EDR/DFIR tooling restoring a quarantined sample onto a lab host
  • Backup/restore software rehydrating a previously-infected user Library
  • Analyst manually copying the IOC file for reverse-engineering on a monitored host
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged macOS runner, confirm the plist exists under ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and check `launchctl list` for the zsh.profiler service and the com.apple.Terminal/profiler support dir. 2) Contain: unload the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout / remove plist), kill the profiler binary, isolate the host, and rotate all Apple signing material and CI secrets that lived on it. 3) Hunt: pivot to the 89.36.224.5 C2 UC and the @velora-dex/sdk install UC on the same DeviceId, and sweep the macOS fleet for the plist name and payload hashes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/" and FileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist")
   or FolderPath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"
   or SHA256 in ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270","0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.Terminal.profiler.plist" and TargetFilePath has "/LaunchAgents/")
   or TargetFilePath has "com.apple.Terminal/profiler"
   or TargetFileSHA256 in ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270","0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node install-time payload: package manager spawning curl/launchctl/osascript on a runner AIExploitation Medium
Behavioural catch for the Velora-class TTP where importing a poisoned npm package makes node call child_process.exec() to download and persist a payload. Surfaces node/npm/yarn/pnpm/bun spawning curl, wget, osascript, chmod or launchctl during a build — catching variants and future-versioned repackages the static IOCs miss. Rationale: Models the corroborated execution mechanism (dist/index.js calling child_process.exec() to curl a shell script then launchctl-persist) as a parent/child pivot, so it catches the campaign's behaviour beyond the pinned version/IOCs. Kept as hunting because legit postinstall scripts also spawn curl. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://phoenix.security/velora-dex-sdk-supply-chain-compromise-build-pipeline-injection-delivers-macos-persistent-implant/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm postinstall scripts (node-sass, node-gyp, puppeteer, esbuild) that curl/wget a prebuilt binary
  • Build scripts that chmod +x downloaded CLI tools
  • macOS packaging steps invoking osascript for notarization/UI prompts
  • Corporate proxy bootstrap scripts run under node during CI setup
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","githubusercontent.com","nodejs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line — a curl/wget to an unfamiliar host, a launchctl load of an unknown plist, or chmod +x on a freshly-downloaded file is malicious; a fetch to a known package CDN (github.com, npmjs.org) is likely benign. 2) Contain: if the destination or plist is unrecognised, isolate the runner and rotate its secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the downloaded host/IP against the C2 UC (89.36.224.5) and check for the launchctl-persistence plist on the same host; diff the repo lockfile for newly-added dependencies.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm","bun")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","osascript","launchctl","chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud worm artifacts written on GitHub Actions runner (shai-hulud-workflow.yml / bundle.js) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the self-replicating Shai-Hulud npm worm's on-disk artifacts as they appear on a compromised runner: the shai-hulud-workflow.yml propagation workflow and the known malicious bundle.js payload hash. Distinct filesystem pivot from the Velora backdoor detections. Rationale: shai-hulud-workflow.yml is the worm's signature propagation artifact and 46faab8ab153...628f09 is the documented malicious bundle.js SHA-256, both corroborated by Unit42, Wiz and Datadog Security Labs — filesystem IOCs with no legitimate reason to exist on a runner. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally checking out an infected repo to a monitored host for analysis
  • IOC-sweep tooling writing sample copies of shai-hulud-workflow.yml to disk during hunting
  • A defensive canary/honeypot repo deliberately seeded with the artifact name
  • Backup restoration of a previously-infected repository working tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path/hash on the runner and identify the initiating process and the repo/workflow it landed in; a true hit means the worm executed and likely harvested tokens. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, revoke npm publish tokens and GitHub PATs the job held, and remove any pushed 'shai-hulud' branch / shai-hulud-workflow.yml from affected repos before it self-propagates. 3) Hunt: enumerate packages published by the compromised token, search for repos with the description marker 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming', and sweep all runners for the workflow filename and bundle.js hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or SHA256 == "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "shai-hulud-workflow.yml"
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "46faab8ab153fae6e80e7cca38eab363075bb524edd79e42269217a083628f09"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or SHA1 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d") or MD5 in~ ("0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0a8ab3d16b12d3a453ee5a3208fe04744ad54514ef8ea27bb8fe32679efad270", "0b028b781950641818800fee2b4bf68e4ef2bcee53fe71a21755275ba108783d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised @velora-dex/sdk npm package (9.4.1/9.4.2) installed on CI runner AIDelivery High
Hunts for the known-trojanized @velora-dex/sdk package landing in node_modules on a macOS/Windows/Linux build runner. Version 9.4.1 injected a base64 loader into dist/index.js that fires on import and pulls a macOS Go RAT (MiniRAT); 9.4.2 was the hurried revert — presence of either on a runner warrants review. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package path '@velora-dex/sdk' confirmed by Corgea, safedep and StepSecurity; on an ephemeral CI runner any occurrence of this known-bad dependency is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://github.com/VeloraDEX/sdk/issues/233
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or internal IR team detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • A pinned lockfile deliberately holding 9.4.2 (reverted) for regression testing
  • Mirror/proxy cache warming that pre-fetches many package versions including these
  • A developer reproducing the advisory locally to confirm exposure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("cape.exe","procmon.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the repo/workflow that pulled @velora-dex/sdk and the exact version from the lockfile; check the runner's outbound connections to 89.36.224.5 in the same job window. 2) Contain: fail/cancel the pipeline, rotate every secret the job could touch (Apple signing certs, App Store Connect keys, Windows code-signing certs, OIDC/cloud tokens), and pin the dependency to a known-good pre-9.4.1 version or the vendor-verified fix. 3) Hunt: sweep all runners and developer macOS hosts for MiniRAT launchctl persistence and for egress to 89.36.224.5 / 216.126.225.129.

| where FileName endswith ".js" or FileName =~ "package.json"

| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to MiniRAT C2 89.36.224.5 (Velora SDK backdoor) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any outbound connection from a runner or build host to 89.36.224.5, the C2 that the injected @velora-dex/sdk loader contacts to fetch its architecture-specific macOS shell-script/Go RAT stager. A hard IOC — no legitimate build should reach this host. Rationale: 89.36.224.5 is the confirmed MiniRAT stager/C2 host (Corgea, safedep) referenced by the article's Velora SDK compromise; a single hard-IOC destination match needs no behavioural qualifier. Cross-checked against: • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor • https://safedep.io/malicious-velora-dex-sdk-npm-compromised-rat/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning service that actively probes known C2 IPs from a monitored host
  • IR sandbox detonation of the sample with live network
  • Security team reproducing the advisory to validate blast radius
  • Shared NAT egress where a non-runner host on the same egress IP is the real source (verify DeviceName/src)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (expect node/npm-spawned sh/curl) and whether @velora-dex/sdk is in the job's dependency tree. 2) Contain: block 89.36.224.5 at egress/firewall, isolate the runner/host, and rotate all secrets the pipeline exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot to launchctl persistence (MiniRAT) and to Megalodon C2 216.126.225.129:8443 across the fleet; review recent installs of @velora-dex/sdk org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.36.224.5"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.36.224.5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI runner egress to Megalodon secret-exfil C2 216.126.225.129:8443 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound connections to 216.126.225.129 (notably TCP 8443), the confirmed Megalodon C2 that received compressed archives of harvested CI secrets, cloud creds, SSH keys and OIDC tokens via HTTPS POST across 5,500+ repos. Any runner reaching this host indicates active secret exfiltration. Rationale: 216.126.225.129:8443 is the corroborated Megalodon HTTPS-POST exfil C2 (StepSecurity, safedep, Phoenix); a destination-IP match is a hard IOC requiring no behavioural context. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/megalodon-mass-github-actions-secret-exfiltration-across-5-500-public-repositories • https://safedep.io/megalodon-mass-github-repo-backdooring-ci-workflows/ • https://phoenix.security/megalodon-ci-github-actions-workflow-poisoning-credential-harvesting/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI enrichment scanner probing the known C2 from a monitored host
  • IR sandbox detonation with live egress
  • Shared-egress NAT attributing another host's traffic to a runner (validate src/DeviceName)
  • Deliberate purple-team replay of the Megalodon workflow payload
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the runner/repo and confirm whether an injected workflow (e.g. SysDiag / Optimize-Build, forged authors build-bot/auto-ci/ci-bot/pipeline-bot) or malicious dependency initiated the connection; capture bytes sent. 2) Contain: block 216.126.225.129, cancel the pipeline, and treat every secret reachable by that job as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: review GitHub Actions workflow files for base64 bash payloads POSTing to :8443, enumerate other repos with the same injected workflow, and correlate with @velora-dex/sdk installs and 89.36.224.5 egress.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr == "216.126.225.129"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

MiniRAT launchctl persistence established during macOS CI build AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for launchctl registering a LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon during a build, spawned from a shell/node/curl parent — the persistence step MiniRAT uses after the @velora-dex/sdk loader drops its arch-specific Go binary. Ephemeral GitHub-hosted macOS runners should never establish OS-level persistence mid-job. Rationale: Maps the MiniRAT launchctl-persistence step (StepSecurity/iru) to the parent chain (node-spawned shell → launchctl load) that a stager uses; on ephemeral runners any mid-build persistence is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/velora-dex-sdk-compromised-on-npm-malicious-version-drops-macos-backdoor-via-launchctl-persistence • https://www.iru.com/blog/minirat • https://corgea.com/research/velora-dex-sdk-npm-minirat-macos-backdoor
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Xcode/fastlane or Homebrew setup steps that legitimately load helper LaunchAgents during app-signing jobs
  • Self-hosted macOS runner bootstrap scripts registering the runner service via launchctl
  • Rosetta/simulator tooling loading daemons on first run
  • Developer macOS host installing a legitimate background service via a shell installer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "actions.runner" and ProcessCommandLine !has "com.github.actions" and ProcessCommandLine !has "fastlane"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the launchctl target plist path and the referenced program binary; confirm the grandparent traces to node/npm and whether @velora-dex/sdk is present or 89.36.224.5 was contacted. 2) Contain: kill the persistence item (launchctl bootout / unload), quarantine the dropped binary, isolate the host, and rotate signing certs/keys handled by that runner. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for plist writes to ~/Library/LaunchAgents or /Library/LaunchDaemons during builds and pivot to the two campaign C2 IPs across all macOS hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "launchctl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "launchctl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("load","bootstrap","submit")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","zsh","node","curl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-58644")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.

npm/node lifecycle script fetching Bun runtime from github.com/oven-sh/bun AIInstallation High
Detects an npm preinstall/postinstall lifecycle script (node.exe parented by npm) reaching out to github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases to download the Bun v1.3.13 runtime. This is the exact bootstrap behaviour of the TeamPCP @bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 payload (bw_setup.js Stage-1) and is highly anomalous on developer endpoints because legitimate JS projects rarely pull Bun via a package-install hook. Rationale: Article explicitly names github.com/oven-sh/bun and Bun v1.3.13 as the runtime downloaded by Stage-1 bw_setup.js during npm preinstall — pairing the github.com/oven-sh/bun URL token with an npm-family parent process is a near-zero-FP signature on production endpoints (developer laptops will produce occasional FPs, hence the parent-process pinning). Cross-checked against Socket and Checkmarx advisories listed below. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/teampcp-bitwarden-cli-supply-chain • https://checkmarx.com/blog/checkmarx-supply-chain-incident-april-2026/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally installing Bun via an npm/yarn install script on a workstation
  • CI/CD build agent (GitHub Actions/Jenkins) running 'curl ... github.com/oven-sh/bun/install.sh | bash' in a job
  • Internal devtool wrapper that bootstraps a Bun toolchain on first run
  • Open-source project benchmark suites that download Bun in their install step
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "jenkins" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "runner\\_work" and DeviceName !startswith "build-" and DeviceName !startswith "ci-" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\actions-runner\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full process tree (npm/node parent → downloader child → Bun URL) and the downloaded artifact's SHA256. Check whether the package the user just installed is on the published TeamPCP IOC list (@bitwarden/cli@2026.4.0 and any sibling Checkmarx packages). Inspect npm cache (~/.npm/_cacache and %AppData%\npm-cache) for the offending package and its preinstall script. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host, rotate every credential reachable from it (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud CLI creds, SSH keys, .env secrets, Docker/kubeconfig), revoke any GitHub PAT touched in the last 30 days, and block egress to audit.checkmarx[.]cx + 94.154.172[.]43 at the perimeter. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the user's npm/GitHub identity for new public repos containing the string 'Shai-Hulud: The Third Coming', then sweep the org for any other host that downloaded github.com/oven-sh/bun via an npm parent in the last 30 days.
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe"]);
// Process-tree pivot — npm parent spawning a downloader child with Bun URL on the command line
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents)
    | where FileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage  = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd    = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage = FileName,
              ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
// Network pivot — same process families connecting to github.com for the Bun release tarball
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "github.com" and (RemoteUrl has "oven-sh/bun" or RemoteUrl has "bun-windows" or RemoteUrl has "bun-linux" or RemoteUrl has "bun-darwin")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (downloaderChildren)
    | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (npmParents) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              InitImage   = InitiatingProcessFileName,
              InitCmd     = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildImage  = "<network-egress>", ChildCmd = RemoteUrl, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256;
union ProcHits, NetHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let bunUrlIndicators = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun", "oven-sh/bun/releases", "bun-windows-x64", "bun-linux-x64", "bun-darwin"]);
let npmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npm","node","yarn","pnpm","npx"]);
let downloaderChildren = dynamic(["node.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","pwsh.exe","node","curl","wget","bun","bash","sh","pwsh"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren) or ParentProcessName has_any (downloaderChildren)
| where (ParentProcessName has_any (npmParents) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (npmParents))
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (bunUrlIndicators)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  selection_child:

  - CI agent installing Bun in a build pipeline (scope detection to dev workstations or scope out CI hosts)
level: high
