TuxBot Telnet/ADB scanner fan-out (credential brute-force propagation) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a single host spraying outbound connections to many public destinations on the Telnet (23/2323) and Android Debug Bridge (5555) ports — the working infection vector of TuxBot's Telnet scanner (1,496 credential pairs) and ADB scanner. High-fidelity because near-zero legitimate endpoints fan out across these IoT-specific ports. Rationale: Targets TuxBot's confirmed working infection vector — the Telnet scanner (1,496 cred pairs) plus ADB (5555) scanner — via a fan-out threshold on the exact scanner ports; ports 23/2323/5555 have essentially no benign endpoint fan-out, making the volume signal high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-tuxbot-v3-iot-botnet-uses-llm-generated-code/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rumble) sweeping the estate on Telnet/ADB ports
  • Shodan-style internet-wide research scanner running from a sanctioned host
  • Network/asset-discovery tool enumerating IoT/OT gear on 23/2323
  • Mobile-device test lab legitimately probing ADB 5555 across many devices
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.0.5","10.20.0.6")   // approved vuln-scanner source IPs — replace with your scanner allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is not a sanctioned scanner (check asset inventory / scanner allowlist) and review the initiating process and destination geo-spread. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network and block egress on 23/2323/5555; if it is an unmanaged IoT device, quarantine its switch port/VLAN. 3) Hunt: check the same host for C2 to the UC1 IPs/domain and for the SHA256 71dfbb… (UC4); pull authentication logs on any internal targets it reached on port 23 for successful weak-credential logons.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionFailed")
| where RemotePort in (23, 2323, 5555)   // Telnet, alt-Telnet, Android Debug Bridge scanners
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // botnet scanner sprays thousands; >100 distinct public IoT ports/day is abnormal for one endpoint
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (23, 2323, 5555)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort), Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DeviceVendor
| where DistinctTargets > 100   // fan-out threshold for IoT scanner behaviour
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=23 OR RemotePort=2323 OR RemotePort=5555)
| cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4, negate=true)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctTargets))
| DistinctTargets > 100
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (23,2323,5555) by All_Traffic.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 100
| sort - distinct_targets
TuxBot fallback C2 via digikalas.online DGA subdomains and DNS TXT queries AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts TuxBot's fall-back C2 channels: DNS lookups to the developer domain digikalas.online (and algorithmically-generated subdomains like newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online) and DNS TXT queries used as a covert command channel. Article-specific because digikalas.online is the confirmed live operator domain and DNS TXT / SHA512-DGA are named fall-back mechanisms. Rationale: Keys on the confirmed live operator domain digikalas.online (resolving on Arvan Cloud) and the named SHA512-DGA / DNS-TXT fall-back channels; the leaked subdomain newtuxdev.sevielw.digikalas.online proves the actor uses multi-label subdomains under this parent, so any resolution is high-value. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://securityonline.info/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1568.002 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign DNS TXT lookups for SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification by mail servers and security tools
  • Domain-monitoring/threat-intel platforms actively resolving digikalas.online for tracking
  • Certificate/ACME validation issuing TXT queries at scale
  • Passive-DNS or brand-protection crawlers enumerating the parent domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("named","dnsmasq","systemd-resolved") and RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate the two signals — any hit on digikalas.online is high-priority; for raw TXT queries, filter out mail servers and confirm the querying process is not a mail/security service. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block digikalas.online and its subdomains at the resolver and isolate any endpoint that resolved it. 3) Hunt: correlate the client IP with UC1 C2 connections and UC2 scanner fan-out; if beaconing intervals appear, capture and decode the TXT responses for encoded commands and pivot on any new resolved IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "digikalas.online"
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".digikalas.online")[0])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, Subdomain, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "digikalas.online" or QueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), QueryTypes = make_set(QueryTypeName), DistinctNames = dcount(Name), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by ClientIP, Name
| order by Queries desc

TuxBot/Akiru known ELF sample execution and drop (SHA256 pivot) AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of the confirmed TuxBot v3 Evolution debug sample (SHA256 71dfbb17…), the x86_64 build with symbols submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20. Article-specific single-hash pivot for the recovered bot binary, including its habit of hiding under a dot-prefixed filename. Rationale: Single confirmed IOC — the SHA256 71dfbb17…, the x86_64 debug build submitted to VirusTotal on 2026-01-20; an exact-hash match is unambiguous and the union covers both drop (FileWritten) and execution. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tuxbot-v3-evolution-iot-botnet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tuxbot-v3-evolution-shows-signs-of-llm.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1564.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or reverse-engineer detonating the known sample in a managed sandbox
  • EDR/AV telemetry from a quarantine or research VLAN where the sample is retained for study
  • Threat-intel platform hashing an archived copy during an automated enrichment sweep
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned analysis VM; capture the full path (watch for a dot-prefixed hidden filename) and the parent process that dropped/launched it. 2) Contain: isolate the device, kill and quarantine the binary, and preserve it plus any persistence entries for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for sibling GCC 14.2.0 production builds; pivot the host onto UC1 (C2 IPs/domain), UC2 (scanner fan-out) and UC3 (DGA/TXT DNS) to scope the infection stage.
let badhash = "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d";
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == badhash | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or SHA1 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d") or MD5 in~ ("71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71dfbb171eca4ef9d02ff630b56e5283bbef7b375d4dbe9e8c9531bef312fa8d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot 'Apple Sync' scheduled task maintaining reverse SSH tunnel forwarding RDP AIInstallation High
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot's persistence: a scheduled task named 'Apple Sync' that re-establishes a reverse SSH tunnel forwarding the local RDP (3389) port to the attacker every hour. Also catches the ssh.exe reverse-forward (-R ... 3389) invocation itself. Both are unique to this campaign's back-connection stage. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim task name 'Apple Sync' (article code block) plus the ssh reverse-forward of RDP/3389 described in the back-connection stage — both are campaign-unique. Cross-checked against Kaspersky press release and The Hacker News write-up confirming the SSH-tunnel/RDP mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1572 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DevOps/SRE reverse SSH tunnels for jump-host access
  • IT tooling that schedules ssh port-forwards for remote support
  • A sysadmin genuinely naming a task 'Apple Sync' for iCloud/Apple sync (rare on Windows servers)
  • Bastion/tunnel software (autossh) creating -R forwards to internal hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("autossh.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bastion","jumphost"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full schtasks/ssh command line and the InitiatingProcess chain; confirm the -R forward target is an external/attacker IP and the local port is 3389. Check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat and a newly-created RDP user. 2) Contain: delete the 'Apple Sync' task, kill ssh.exe, block the remote tunnel IP at the firewall, and disable/network-isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep for termsrv.dll modification, HDUtil.exe, extl.exe, and additions to 'Remote Desktop Users' across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "Apple Sync")
     or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R" and ProcessCommandLine has "3389")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "Apple Sync")
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-R" and CommandLine has "3389")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot termsrv.dll patch enabling concurrent RDP sessions AIInstallation High
Hunts OkoBot's replacement of the legitimate C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll with a patched copy that permits multiple concurrent RDP sessions. Flags any write/modify/delete of termsrv.dll by a process other than the Windows servicing stack (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker/msiexec). Rationale: Uses the verbatim termsrv.dll code block and the article's explicit description of replacing the legitimate DLL with a patched one for multi-RDP. Excluding the servicing stack (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker/poqexec) removes the only legitimate writers, so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows cumulative/quality update replacing termsrv.dll via TrustedInstaller (excluded)
  • Legit RDP-wrapper / concurrent-session tools used intentionally by IT (RDPWrap)
  • Backup/restore or system-image tooling rewriting System32
  • Antivirus quarantine/restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "WinSxS")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the new termsrv.dll hash/signature against the Microsoft-shipped version for the OS build; identify the writing process and its parent. 2) Contain: restore the clean termsrv.dll from WinSxS/backup, kill the writer, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the 'Apple Sync' task, new local RDP users, firewall RDP allow rules, and inbound RDP logons (4624 type 10) around the modification time.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","msiexec.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "termsrv.dll"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","msiexec.exe","poqexec.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot HDUtil launcher execution (target/nouac) with HWID guardrail AIInstallation High
Hunts the OkoBot HDUtil launcher, a VMProtect-obfuscated module the SSH bot uses to deploy payloads via its 'target' command (with optional 'nouac'/'noattach'/'user=' and enumeration commands 'enumsessions'/'enumadapters'). HDUtil gates execution on %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat, so hwid.dat file activity is a corroborating signal. Rationale: Anchored on the launcher binary name HDUtil.exe and its exact command verbs (target, nouac, noattach, enumsessions, enumadapters) from the article's command table, plus the %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat HWID guardrail. These strings are wholly campaign-specific and won't collide with commodity tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1480 T1027 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate utility coincidentally named HDUtil.exe (verify signer/path)
  • Hard-drive vendor tooling with 'HDUtil' branding running benign commands
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned sandbox
  • Backup/imaging software passing a 'target' argument (verify the binary is HDUtil.exe specifically)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Seagate","Western Digital","Microsoft") and FolderPath has "Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the HDUtil.exe signer/path is not a known vendor tool, capture the SHA256, and check for %PROGRAMDATA%\hwid.dat and the payload named after 'target' (e.g. extl.exe). 2) Contain: kill HDUtil.exe and its children, quarantine the binary, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent (SSH bot / TeviRAT), search the fleet for HDUtil.exe and hwid.dat, and review recent SFTP/SSH tunnel connections.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("target","nouac","noattach","enumsessions","enumadapters") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("target","nouac")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\HDUtil.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\HDUtil.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("target","nouac","noattach","enumsessions","enumadapters")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot UAC bypass via auto-elevated msconfig.exe spawning payload AIExploitation Medium
Hunts OkoBot's HDUtil 'nouac' UAC bypass, which abuses Windows RPC and the auto-elevating msconfig.exe (Project Zero 2019 technique) to run a payload at High integrity without a UAC prompt. Flags msconfig.exe spawning a non-standard, elevated child process. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit statement that HDUtil's 'nouac' option bypasses UAC via Windows RPC and auto-elevated msconfig.exe. msconfig.exe rarely spawns arbitrary elevated children, so a High/System-integrity child of msconfig.exe is a strong (if noisier) escalation signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1548.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin launching a tool from the msconfig 'Tools' tab (Event Viewer, Command Prompt, etc.)
  • Legitimate troubleshooting where msconfig is used to launch system utilities
  • Software installers that call msconfig for boot configuration
  • Endpoint management scripts interacting with System Configuration
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Windows\\System32\\","\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\") and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the msconfig grandparent chain — was msconfig itself launched by explorer/user, or by a script/SSH-bot context? Check whether the child is a signed system tool or an unknown binary in a temp/ProgramData path. 2) Contain: if the child is unsigned/untrusted, kill it, quarantine, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with HDUtil.exe target/nouac executions and hwid.dat on the same host, and review for follow-on payloads (extl.exe, keylogger, stealer).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msconfig.exe"
| where ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("High","System")
| where FileName !in~ ("conhost.exe","WerFault.exe","msconfig.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessIntegrityLevel, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\msconfig.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\WerFault.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot browser-extension loader extl.exe deployed via HDUtil AIInstallation High
Hunts OkoBot's first SFTP-delivered module: extl.exe, the browser-extensions loader (the injector chain that sideloads Rilide-style crypto-theft extensions), executed via '.\HDUtil.exe target extl.exe'. Detects extl.exe execution and its HDUtil parentage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim invocation '.\HDUtil.exe target extl.exe' and the module name extl.exe from the Browser-extensions-loader section. The HDUtil→extl.exe parent-child pair is a distinctive, high-fidelity pivot unique to OkoBot. Ledger/Trezor extension-injection objective corroborated by The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/okobot-malware-framework-injects-seed.html
ATT&CKT1176 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated internal tool named extl.exe (verify path/signer/hash)
  • Developer build artifact abbreviated 'extl' (check parentage — should NOT be HDUtil.exe)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample
  • Browser enterprise-extension deployment tooling (parent is a management agent, not HDUtil.exe)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture extl.exe SHA256 and confirm the parent is HDUtil.exe or a script chain; inspect Chromium 'User Data\*\Extensions' and Local State/Secure Preferences for newly-added unpacked/unsigned extensions. 2) Contain: kill extl.exe, remove the injected extension(s), reset affected browser profiles, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to SeedHunter/keylogger/stealer modules and check crypto-wallet apps (Ledger Live, Trezor Suite) and browser wallet extensions for tampering.

| where FileName =~ "extl.exe" or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HDUtil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "extl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688

OkoBot RDP back-connection: local RDP user creation + firewall opening AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot enabling attacker RDP access: adding a user to the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, opening firewall ports for inbound RDP, and flipping fDenyTSConnections to 0. Any one of these on an endpoint outside a change window is suspicious; together they map the back-connection sequence. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's back-connection steps: create a user in the 'Remote Desktop Users' group, open firewall ports for inbound RDP, and enable RDP (fDenyTSConnections). Bundling the three complementary commands raises fidelity while each remains article-grounded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.kaspersky.com/about/press-releases/kaspersky-reveals-a-new-malicious-framework-targeting-cryptocurrency-users-with-the-use-of-okospyware
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1021.001 T1562.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk enabling RDP for legitimate remote support
  • GPO/Intune baselines toggling fDenyTSConnections or RDP firewall rules
  • New admin onboarding added to Remote Desktop Users
  • RMM tooling opening 3389 during provisioning
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe","mmc.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("gpscript.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/parent — legitimate config comes from GPO/Intune/admin sessions; OkoBot comes from an SSH-bot/script chain. Enumerate any newly-added RDP user and its creation time. 2) Contain: remove the rogue account, close the firewall rule, restore fDenyTSConnections=1, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate with the 'Apple Sync' task, termsrv.dll modification, and inbound RDP logons (4624 type 10) from external IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "localgroup" and ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and ProcessCommandLine has "/add")
     or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "3389")
     or (FileName =~ "netsh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "advfirewall" and ProcessCommandLine has "Remote Desktop")
     or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\net.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\net1.exe") and CommandLine has "localgroup" and CommandLine has "Remote Desktop Users" and CommandLine has "/add"
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\netsh.exe" and CommandLine has "advfirewall" and (CommandLine has "3389" or CommandLine has "Remote Desktop"))
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "fDenyTSConnections")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OkoBot disabling Windows Defender notifications via registry AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OkoBot SSH bot suppressing Defender alerts to enable stealthy module delivery, done via a registry modification. Detects setting DisableNotifications/DisableEnhancedNotifications under Windows Defender Security Center by a non-installer process. Rationale: Grounded in the article's statement that the SSH bot 'disables Windows Defender notifications via a registry modification' before delivering modules. Scoping to the Defender Security Center Notifications keys with a value of 1 and excluding installer/GPO writers keeps this targeted. Falcon left empty — FDR's registry telemetry (AsepValueUpdate) only covers autostart keys, not this notification value. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/okobot-framework-targets-cryptocurrency-wallets/120660/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise GPO/Intune policy disabling Defender toast notifications org-wide
  • MDM baseline hardening that suppresses Security Center pop-ups
  • Third-party AV installer taking over Defender and muting notifications
  • Admin manually reducing notification noise on a jump box
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("gpscript.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("intune","CCM","SCCM"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process — policy comes from gpscript/msiexec/MDM; OkoBot comes from an SSH-bot/script chain or an unsigned binary. Check timing against any legitimate policy push. 2) Contain: revert the value, re-enable Defender notifications, and isolate the host if the writer is untrusted. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on OkoBot activity on the same host — HDUtil.exe, extl.exe, 'Apple Sync' task, termsrv.dll patch, and SFTP module delivery.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender Security Center\Notifications" or RegistryValueName in~ ("DisableNotifications","DisableEnhancedNotifications")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","gpscript.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"Windows Defender Security Center\Notifications" or RegistryValue in~ ("DisableNotifications","DisableEnhancedNotifications")
| where RegistryValueData in ("1","0x1")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("msiexec.exe","gpscript.exe","MsMpEng.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46817")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
